evidence.snippet: These data provide the first mechanistic insights into the pathogenesis of BLBS from a human-derived model of neurodevelopment
evidence.explanation: The hyper-deposition model rests on a single human-derived model system, which is why it is recorded as emerging rather than canonical.

hypotheses/0.description: Proposes that the H3-3B disease allele acts by increasing H3-3B expression and driving excess incorporation of H3.3 into nucleosomes, so that the primary lesion is too much variant histone in chromatin rather than a loss of histone function. Demonstrated so far for a single allele (p.Leu48Arg) in one isogenic iPSC series; whether it generalises to tail-domain, core-domain and stop-loss BLBS2 alleles is untested, and it sits alongside the alternative view that different variants act through heterogeneous local mechanisms (impaired chaperone binding, altered protein stability, disrupted DNA contact).

evidence.snippet: Since these variables do not account for all BLBS phenotypic variability, these findings suggest that additional factors may play a role in modifying the phenotypes of affected individuals.
evidence.explanation: The authors explicitly state that gene, variant location and sex leave BLBS phenotypic variability unexplained.

open_questions/0.rationale: The two BLBS entities exist because two genes are involved, not because two proteins are. The only known differences are in untranslated and coding sequence, which alter expression pattern and level. Cohort data show gene-dependent frequency differences (seizures 59% vs 45%; genital anomalies 28% vs 17%; delayed walking 65% vs 85%), so the paralogs are not interchangeable, but the mechanism converting a paralog-level expression difference into these phenotype shifts is unknown. Resolving it determines whether BLBS1 and BLBS2 should remain separate entities or be lumped.

evidence.snippet: Three variant constructs (p.R129H, p.M121I, and p.I52N) showed significant decrease in protein expression, while one variant (p.R41C) accumulated at greater levels than wild-type control.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates opposite-direction effects on H3.3 abundance among BLBS alleles, which is the substance of this gap.

open_questions/1.rationale: Functional data point in different directions: some constructs reduce H3.3 protein levels while another accumulates above wild-type; one increases chaperone binding; and the one allele studied in a human neural model (p.L48R) increases H3-3B expression and nucleosomal H3.3. Whether these are variations on one theme or genuinely different mechanisms determines whether a single therapeutic strategy could serve the whole disorder.

evidence.snippet: These data suggest that the mechanism of germline mutations are distinct from cancer-associated somatic histone mutations but may converge on control of cell proliferation.
evidence.explanation: States the unresolved convergence between germline and somatic H3.3 mechanisms that motivates this gap.

evidence.snippet: the value of ongoing translational work to address the outstanding question of cancer predisposition for individuals living with germline histonopathies
evidence.explanation: The pan-histonopathy cohort names cancer predisposition as an explicitly outstanding question.

open_questions/2.rationale: Patient fibroblasts, including H3F3B p.G34V lines, proliferate faster than controls and up-regulate mitosis genes, yet the founding 46-patient cohort had congenital anomalies without malignancies and the community-wide cancer incidence across germline histonopathies sits at 1%. Somatic p.G34V is oncogenic only in combination with ATRX/DAXX and TP53 lesions, suggesting the germline context lacks the required cooperating hits, or that developmental timing and cell of origin gate transformation.

evidence.snippet: BLBS was initially categorized as a progressive neurodegenerative syndrome caused by de novo heterozygous variants in either H3-3A or H3-3B
evidence.explanation: Documents the initial neurodegenerative framing that the expanded neurodevelopmental characterisation now sits alongside.

evidence.snippet: histonopathy-associated phenotypes change throughout the lifespan, necessitating longitudinal re-evaluation
evidence.explanation: Independent argument that the natural history is not yet settled and requires longitudinal study.

open_questions/3.rationale: BLBS was first described as a progressive neurodegenerative syndrome, and GeneReviews lists loss of milestones, worsening gait, spasticity and camptocormia. But the expanded cohort reframed the disorder as primarily neurodevelopmental, and some individuals show resolving rather than progressive hypotonia. No longitudinal imaging or biomarker study has established whether neuronal loss actually occurs. The answer changes both prognostic counselling and trial endpoint selection.

evidence.snippet: A dominant zebrafish model (p.D123N) derived from a forward genetic screen has been previously reported with craniofacial abnormalities, which were replicated in our patient cohort
evidence.explanation: Confirms that the craniofacial model evidence comes from the h3f3a paralog, which is the substance of the translational mismatch.

open_questions/4.rationale: The craniofacial and glial arms of the mechanism rest substantially on a zebrafish h3f3a model (dominant p.D123N and homozygous db1092 alleles). Since the whole basis for splitting BLBS1 from BLBS2 is a paralog-level difference in expression rather than protein sequence, a model built on the other paralog cannot by construction test paralog-specific effects, and zebrafish h3f3 gene-family structure differs from the human two-gene arrangement. The craniofacial phenotype may therefore be attributable to total H3.3 dosage rather than to anything specific to H3-3B.

evidence.snippet: they more strikingly highlight data gaps that confound the identification of phenotypic patterns at this time.
evidence.explanation: The pan-histonopathy phenotyping analysis identifies uncertainty in the phenotypic patterns themselves, motivating association confirmation before assigning mechanisms to variably reported BLBS features.

evidence.snippet: Both H3F3B and H3F3A are expressed ubiquitously, during development and throughout life, with relatively high levels of expression in the brain, testes, ovaries, and uterus
evidence.explanation: The expression pattern makes multi-organ involvement plausible while leaving the tissue-specific mechanisms unstudied, which is the substance of this gap.

open_questions/5.rationale: All mechanistic work on BLBS to date concerns chromatin, neural differentiation, proliferation and the neural crest; no study has examined how the variant histone perturbs cardiac, genitourinary, skeletal-growth, endocrine, dermatologic or auditory development. Ubiquitous H3.3 expression — with relatively high levels in testes, ovaries and uterus as well as brain — makes multi-system involvement plausible, but plausibility is not a mechanism, and these phenotypes are deliberately left without causal edges in the pathograph rather than wired to the neurologic endpoint they do not belong to. Three of them are the ones most tempting to wire anyway, because a neurologic-secondary story is easy to tell: constipation may simply follow hypotonia and immobility, scoliosis may be neuromuscular, and the feeding difficulties and poor weight gain may follow oromotor dysfunction and abnormal tone. No source states any of the three for BLBS, so the same standard applies to them as to the rest — and scoliosis and joint hypermobility come from the same musculoskeletal table row of the same cohort at nearly the same frequency (21% and 22%), so treating them differently would be arbitrary. Craniosynostosis is the closest call in this list, since it is a skull-vault phenotype and the entry does model a neural-crest and craniofacial developmental defect; it is left here because no BLBS source links the two, and because the craniofacial evidence is a zebrafish h3f3a result rather than a human one. Association itself also needs evaluation before mechanism: the 2025 pan-histonopathy analysis emphasizes data gaps that confound phenotypic-pattern identification. Thus a recorded cardiac, auditory, genitourinary or endocrine finding should not automatically be treated as an established syndrome-defining association.

evidence.snippet: these experiences are more strongly associated with binge-purge type disorders such as BN, BED, and AN-BP
evidence.explanation: The rapid review identifies an association with childhood trauma and abuse across binge/purge diagnoses; it is not a necessary or sufficient cause of BN.

evidence.snippet: We calculated the functional connectivity of striatal subregions based on the resting-state functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging data of 51 bulimia nervosa patients and 53 healthy women.
evidence.explanation: Defines the primary human imaging cohort.

evidence.snippet: the molecular basis of the striatal RSFC changes observed in our study is unclear
evidence.explanation: The full-text limitation prevents assignment of a measured serotonin or dopamine lesion from these imaging data.

evidence.snippet: Only for the putamen subregions, we observed reduced negative functional connectivity in the prefrontal (bilateral superior and middle frontal gyri) and parietal (right inferior parietal lobe and precuneus) areas.
evidence.explanation: A specific connectivity result, not proof of globally reduced reward activation.

steps/1.description: Human imaging identifies altered striatal, prefrontal, thalamic, sensorimotor and visual network function. Direction varies by network and paradigm, so this is not a uniform reward deficit. Resting-state correlations do not measure neuronal inhibition directly and cannot establish whether findings are causes or consequences of illness.

evidence.snippet: Proband-wise concordance for narrowly defined bulimia was 22.9% in monozygotic and 8.7% in dizygotic twins.
evidence.explanation: Greater monozygotic concordance supports familial genetic liability in this female twin cohort.

evidence.snippet: Risk factors for bulimia included 1) birth after 1960, 2) low paternal care, 3) a history of wide weight fluctuation, dieting, or frequent exercise, 4) a slim ideal body image, 5) low self-esteem, 6) an external locus of control, and 7) high levels of neuroticism.
evidence.explanation: These are associated risk factors, not independently proven causal exposures.

steps/2.description: Familial genetic liability interacts with psychological and social risk factors. Twin and register-based estimates support heritability, but do not establish a single causal gene, a fixed molecular lesion, or genetic determinism.

evidence.snippet: BN is characterized by overvaluation of body weight and shape and recurrent binge-eating
evidence.explanation: Clinical synthesis identifies the central cognitive and behavioral features.

evidence.snippet: follow by addressing the eating disorder psychopathology (for example, the extreme dietary restraint, the concerns about body shape and weight, and the tendency to binge eat in response to difficult thoughts and feelings)
evidence.explanation: Guideline identifies the maintenance processes targeted by CBT.

steps/3.description: Excessive dependence of self-evaluation on shape or weight, restrictive eating rules, and irregular eating contribute to a cognitive-behavioral maintenance model. These are targets of CBT; their relationship to molecular or imaging findings is not an established linear causal sequence.

evidence.snippet: Results supported greater NA preceding binge eating relative to average affect (ES = 0.63) and affect before regular eating (ES = 0.68).
evidence.explanation: The meta-analysis includes several binge-eating diagnoses; it supports an antecedent association rather than BN-specific causal proof.

evidence.snippet: The results indicate that post-binge ratings of negative affect were significantly higher than the pre-binge ratings of negative affect for women in both Study 1-AN and Study 2-BN.
evidence.explanation: Full-text results resolve the opposite direction stated in the abstract. BN results are analyzed separately from AN.

evidence.snippet: the post-binge ratings were made significantly closer in time to the binge-eating episode than the pre-binge ratings
evidence.explanation: Unequal timing limits inference from a simple before/after comparison; binge-only episodes were analyzed.

steps/4.description: Negative affect commonly rises before binge eating. Whether it is lower afterward depends on the sampling time and analysis. In a BN ecological momentary assessment reanalysis, proximal post-binge affect was higher than the earlier pre-binge rating, while modeled trajectories could still decline after an episode. This supports a qualified affect-regulation model, not universal or proven relief from bingeing or purging.

evidence.snippet: consuming an excessive caloric amount in a short period of time, usually a 2-hour period, that the patient feels unable to control
evidence.explanation: Defines the binge event in this clinical review.

steps/5.description: Recurrent episodes involve an objectively large amount of food and a sense of loss of control under DSM criteria. Binge eating also occurs in other eating disorders; the associated compensatory behavior and shape/weight psychopathology define the BN context.

evidence.snippet: its cardinal feature is recurrent binge eating followed by extreme weight control or compensatory behaviours in association with high levels of weight and shape, and other body image and eating, preoccupations.
evidence.explanation: The contemporary primer defines the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: compensatory behaviours, including laxative or diet pill misuse, vomiting or excessive exercise
evidence.explanation: Guideline assessment encompasses multiple forms of compensation.

steps/6.description: Vomiting and laxative or diuretic misuse are purging methods; fasting and excessive exercise are nonpurging compensatory behaviors. Their physical consequences differ. The following electrolyte and acid-exposure pathways specifically concern relevant purging methods.

evidence.snippet: With repetitive vomiting, the esophageal epithelium suffers repeated abnormal exposure to acidic gastric contents and microtrauma.
evidence.explanation: Provides the direct local injury mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Dental erosions are irreversible once they have developed.
evidence.explanation: Separates persistent enamel loss from reversible systemic disturbances.

steps/7.description: Repeated vomiting exposes dental enamel and esophageal mucosa to gastric acid and mechanical injury. Dental erosion may be irreversible. Reflux complaints do not reliably indicate severe endoscopic injury; tears and rupture are uncommon severe complications.

evidence.snippet: Pathology study reveals hypertrophied acinar cells with otherwise preserved architecture without evidence of inflammation.
evidence.explanation: Describes salivary tissue pathology.

evidence.snippet: Isoenzyme studies further demonstrate that the elevations in serum amylase originate from salivary glands as opposed to the pancreas
evidence.explanation: Supports the salivary origin of hyperamylasemia in the studied purging population.

steps/8.description: Vomiting-associated sialadenosis consists of non-inflammatory acinar hypertrophy, usually involving both parotid glands. The precise trigger is uncertain; it must not be equated with inflammatory sialadenitis. Serum amylase elevation may be salivary rather than pancreatic.

evidence.snippet: Electrolytes lost through laxative use include chloride, calcium, bicarbonate, and potassium.
evidence.explanation: Identifies direct losses.

evidence.snippet: acute diarrhea of shorter duration results in a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis
evidence.explanation: Supports the acidosis pathway.

steps/9.description: Acute laxative-induced diarrhea removes bicarbonate and can cause normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Chronic diarrhea with pronounced volume depletion can instead produce secondary hyperaldosteronism and alkalosis; not every purging method produces the same acid-base pattern.

evidence.snippet: Repeated episodes of vomiting can lead to dehydration and subsequent upregulation of the secretion of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone steroid hormone system.
evidence.explanation: Connects volume depletion to compensatory hormonal activation.

evidence.snippet: The majority of patients with bulimia, who vomit only occasionally, will have normal serum electrolytes
evidence.explanation: Explains why normal laboratory findings do not exclude the syndrome.

steps/10.description: Purging can cause loss of sodium chloride, water and potassium. The pattern depends on vomiting, diuretic use or laxative-induced diarrhea and on frequency. Normal electrolytes in intermittent purging do not exclude BN.

evidence.snippet: Aldosterone also promotes renal secretion of potassium into the urine and thus hypokalemia.
evidence.explanation: Defines a key renal mechanism.

evidence.snippet: This mechanism of potassium loss is actually a larger contributor to the hypokalemia than the actual gastrointestinal or urinary loses from the behaviors themselves.
evidence.explanation: Distinguishes secondary renal loss from direct loss.

evidence.snippet: Intravascular volume depletion resulting from the loss of sodium chloride increases the resorption of bicarbonate within the proximal renal tubule, preventing its loss in the urine
evidence.explanation: Explains maintenance of alkalosis.

steps/11.description: Volume depletion activates renin-angiotensin-aldosterone signaling. Aldosterone promotes sodium retention at the expense of renal potassium and hydrogen loss. Vomiting-related acid loss, volume contraction and renal bicarbonate retention sustain hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Renal potassium loss can exceed the direct gastrointestinal loss.

evidence.snippet: The resultant hypokalaemia can result in a prolonged QTc interval putting the patient at risk for significant arrhythmias resulting in syncope and palpitations.
evidence.explanation: Links potassium disturbance to cardiac electrical risk.

steps/12.description: Purging-related hypokalemia and acid-base disturbance can prolong repolarization and predispose to serious ventricular arrhythmias, including torsades de pointes. These are secondary medical complications, not a defining inherited long-QT syndrome.

evidence.snippet: The reason is that the serum aldosterone levels remain high, causing salt and water retention even though the patient is no longer losing fluid, as the purging has ceased.
evidence.explanation: Explains edema after cessation.

evidence.snippet: can result in severe peripheral edema formation especially if the patient with bulimia is given intravenous saline-containing fluids in a rapid manner
evidence.explanation: Documents the fluid-treatment interaction.

steps/13.description: In pseudo-Bartter physiology, aldosterone remains elevated after purging stops. Continued renal sodium retention without ongoing fluid loss can produce rapid edema and distressing weight gain, especially with rapid saline administration. This is acquired physiology, not inherited Bartter syndrome.

evidence.snippet: its cardinal feature is recurrent binge eating followed by extreme weight control or compensatory behaviours
evidence.explanation: Contemporary synthesis supports the combined phenotype.

steps/14.description: Recurrent binge eating with compensatory behavior is the defining pattern. The HPO term captures the combined behavioral phenotype, rather than binge eating in isolation.

evidence.snippet: Self-induced vomiting is the most frequently used purging method
evidence.explanation: Supports vomiting while allowing other methods.

steps/15.description: Self-induced vomiting is a common compensatory method but is not required in every BN presentation.

evidence.snippet: patients showed more frequent occurrence of low values for serum potassium (6.8% vs. 0.9%; p <.05) and chloride (8.1% vs. 0.9%; p <.02).
evidence.explanation: Study of 74 otherwise healthy, medication-free, normal-weight outpatient women with purging BN; these rates are not universal.

steps/16.description: Purging-related hypokalemia may be clinically silent or life-threatening. Frequency depends on setting and behavior; it occurred in 6.8% of otherwise healthy outpatient women in one controlled study.

evidence.snippet: patients showed more frequent occurrence of low values for serum potassium (6.8% vs. 0.9%; p <.05) and chloride (8.1% vs. 0.9%; p <.02).
evidence.explanation: Study of 74 otherwise healthy, medication-free, normal-weight outpatient women with purging BN; these rates are not universal.

steps/17.description: Low chloride can accompany vomiting or other purging losses; 8.1% of women in the selected outpatient study had low serum chloride.

evidence.snippet: Patients with self-induced vomiting or diuretic abuse, or both, have been shown to present with hypokalemia, hypochloremia, and a metabolic alkalosis.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the clinical biochemical pattern.

steps/18.description: Vomiting and volume-depleting diuretic misuse can produce hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis; chronic laxative-associated volume depletion may do likewise.

evidence.snippet: acute diarrhea of shorter duration results in a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis
evidence.explanation: Supports the method-specific complication.

steps/19.description: Shorter-duration laxative-induced diarrhea may produce hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis rather than alkalosis.

evidence.snippet: Hyponatremia can also be present with these 3 purging behaviors.
evidence.explanation: Clinical synthesis describes a possible complication.

steps/20.description: Hyponatremia can accompany purging-related fluid and sodium disturbance; it is not an obligatory finding.

evidence.snippet: Repeated episodes of vomiting can lead to dehydration
evidence.explanation: Supports dehydration.

steps/21.description: Vomiting, laxative misuse or diuretic misuse can cause fluid depletion.

evidence.snippet: Dehydration as a result of repeated episodes of emesis can result in both resting and exertional sinus tachycardia, hypotension, and orthostasis.
evidence.explanation: Supports hemodynamic complications.

steps/22.description: Volume depletion may cause orthostatic hypotension and presyncope.

evidence.snippet: The resultant hypokalaemia can result in a prolonged QTc interval
evidence.explanation: Supports the acquired ECG abnormality.

steps/23.description: Acquired QTc prolongation can develop with hypokalemia; it is not universal or evidence for congenital long-QT disease.

evidence.snippet: The most severe of these is a specific type of ventricular tachycardia known as torsades de pointes that can be fatal
evidence.explanation: Documents a severe arrhythmic complication.

steps/24.description: Electrolyte disturbance can produce clinically important arrhythmias, including torsades de pointes in severe hypokalemia.

evidence.snippet: significant arrhythmias resulting in syncope and palpitations
evidence.explanation: Supports syncope as a complication.

steps/25.description: Syncope may occur with arrhythmia or marked hemodynamic disturbance.

evidence.snippet: can result in severe peripheral edema formation especially if the patient with bulimia is given intravenous saline-containing fluids in a rapid manner
evidence.explanation: Supports the conditional edema phenotype.

steps/26.description: Rapid edema can follow purging cessation because secondary aldosterone elevation persists, especially if fluid replacement is excessive.

evidence.snippet: Dental erosions typically occur on the lingual surface of the maxillary teeth.
evidence.explanation: Defines the distribution of erosion.

evidence.snippet: While there is consensus that bulimic behaviour directly causes dental erosion due to vomiting and acidic food choices, there is less clear evidence for a direct link between bulimia nervosa and dental caries
evidence.explanation: Supports erosion and limits extrapolation to caries.

steps/27.description: Acquired enamel erosion, often on lingual maxillary surfaces, follows acid exposure during vomiting. The broader HPO enamel-morphology term is used because a specific dental-erosion term was not found; developmental enamel hypoplasia would misrepresent this acquired process.

evidence.snippet: The bilateral parotid glands are the glands most commonly involved, but submandibular enlargement may also be seen
evidence.explanation: Specifies the glands involved.

steps/28.description: Usually bilateral non-inflammatory sialadenosis can accompany recurrent vomiting and may become conspicuous after cessation.

evidence.snippet: Isoenzyme studies further demonstrate that the elevations in serum amylase originate from salivary glands as opposed to the pancreas
evidence.explanation: Supports salivary hyperamylasemia.

steps/29.description: Elevated serum amylase can originate from salivary glands in purging presentations; total amylase elevation alone does not establish pancreatitis.

evidence.snippet: Patients who induce vomiting will commonly complain of symptoms consistent with gastroesophageal reflux (GERD), dysphagia, and odynophagia
evidence.explanation: Supports symptomatic reflux.

steps/30.description: Reflux symptoms are reported in vomiting presentations. Symptom severity and endoscopic injury may be discordant.

evidence.snippet: endoscopic evaluation is generally normal or only demonstrates mild esophagitis
evidence.explanation: Keeps the structural finding proportional to the clinical evidence.

steps/31.description: Repeated vomiting can produce esophagitis, although endoscopic findings are often normal or mild.

evidence.snippet: Mallory-Weiss tears commonly present as blood-streaked or tinged emesis or scant coffee ground emesis following recurrent vomiting episodes.
evidence.explanation: Supports the bleeding manifestation.

steps/32.description: Mallory-Weiss tears after repeated retching can cause blood-streaked vomitus; this is a complication rather than a defining feature.

evidence.snippet: A history of prolonged laxative use may also produce a more innocuous reflex constipation.
evidence.explanation: Supports rebound constipation.

evidence.snippet: it is currently speculative as to whether this condition truly develops in those with eating disorders and with use of currently available stimulant laxatives.
evidence.explanation: Limits the stronger historical claim about cathartic colon.

steps/33.description: Constipation may occur during withdrawal from chronic laxative misuse. Permanent cathartic-colon injury with currently used stimulant laxatives remains uncertain.

evidence.snippet: Risk factors for bulimia included 1) birth after 1960, 2) low paternal care, 3) a history of wide weight fluctuation, dieting, or frequent exercise, 4) a slim ideal body image, 5) low self-esteem, 6) an external locus of control, and 7) high levels of neuroticism.
evidence.explanation: Associated risk factors connect liability to the cognitive-behavioral model; the twin study does not establish this causal sequence.

edges/0.description: Familial and psychosocial susceptibility is associated with dieting, slim body ideals and low self-esteem; the direction and intermediates linking these factors remain uncertain.

edges/1.description: Restrictive eating and shape/weight concerns are proposed contributors to the maintenance of binge eating.

edges/2.description: Negative affect is a temporally associated antecedent and proposed trigger; observational assessments do not establish causation.

evidence.snippet: Only for the putamen subregions, we observed reduced negative functional connectivity in the prefrontal (bilateral superior and middle frontal gyri) and parietal (right inferior parietal lobe and precuneus) areas.
evidence.explanation: Cross-sectional connectivity differences are associated with BN, not proof that the imaging finding causes binge eating.

edges/3.description: Altered reward and control networks may relate to binge eating, but cross-sectional imaging cannot determine whether these differences precede illness or result from it.

edges/4.description: Binge episodes are followed by attempts to counter perceived weight gain.

edges/5.description: Binge eating with compensatory behavior constitutes the defining clinical pattern.

edges/6.description: Self-induced vomiting is one compensatory method.

edges/7.description: Vomiting exposes teeth and upper gastrointestinal mucosa to acid and mechanical trauma.

edges/8.description: Recurrent vomiting is associated with sialadenosis; its precise mechanism remains uncertain.

edges/9.description: Vomiting, diarrhea from laxative misuse, and diuretic misuse can deplete fluid and electrolytes.

edges/10.description: Laxative-induced diarrhea can remove bicarbonate and potassium.

evidence.snippet: A history of prolonged laxative use may also produce a more innocuous reflex constipation.
evidence.explanation: Supports rebound constipation.

edges/11.description: Chronic laxative misuse can be followed by rebound constipation on withdrawal; this does not establish permanent cathartic-colon damage.

edges/12.description: Acid exposure erodes enamel.

edges/13.description: Vomiting and sphincter dysfunction can contribute to reflux symptoms.

edges/14.description: Acid exposure can inflame or erode esophageal mucosa.

edges/15.description: Repeated retching can cause bleeding mucosal tears.

edges/16.description: Acinar hypertrophy manifests as gland enlargement.

edges/17.description: Salivary amylase can contribute to increased circulating total amylase.

edges/18.description: Fluid loss can cause dehydration.

edges/19.description: Gastric or other purging-related losses can reduce chloride.

edges/20.description: Sodium and fluid disturbances can produce hyponatremia.

edges/21.description: Reduced circulating volume can cause orthostatic symptoms.

edges/22.description: Volume depletion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

edges/23.description: Renal potassium wasting contributes to hypokalemia.

edges/24.description: Acid loss and renal retention of bicarbonate sustain alkalosis.

edges/25.description: Potassium depletion can disturb cardiac repolarization.

edges/26.description: Persistent aldosterone activity can cause fluid retention when ongoing losses cease.

edges/29.description: Arrhythmia or hemodynamic compromise can cause syncope.

edges/30.description: Retained sodium and water cause edema.

edges/31.description: Fecal bicarbonate loss can produce hyperchloremic acidosis.

evidence.explanation: The rapid review identifies an association with childhood trauma and abuse across binge/purge diagnoses; it is not a necessary or sufficient cause of BN.

edges/32.description: Associated early adversity contributes to the psychosocial risk context; causal direction and mediating mechanisms remain incompletely resolved.

evidence.snippet: The best-fitting model indicated that familial aggregation was due solely to genetic factors with a heritability of liability of 55%.
evidence.explanation: Model-based estimate in the historic female twin cohort.
BN-specific estimate from the published register study, replacing the earlier preprint.

evidence.snippet: We did not account for the inﬂuence of shared environmental factors among close relatives on heritability and genetic correlation estimates.
evidence.explanation: The full-text limitation constrains causal and quantitative interpretation.

evidence.snippet: We identified six BE-associated loci, including loci associated with a higher body mass index and impulse-control behaviors.
evidence.explanation: Indirect evidence from a broad transdiagnostic binge-eating phenotype, not a dedicated BN locus analysis.

genes/0.notes: The 1991 female twin study estimated liability heritability at 55%. A 2025 Danish/Swedish register study estimated BN heritability at 0.39 (95% CI 0.32–0.46). These estimates depend on study design and ascertainment; they are not penetrance or individual predictions. The register study did not account for shared environmental effects and did not identify causal genes. A 2026 GWAS of broadly defined binge-eating behavior includes BN, BED and symptom-level cases; its six loci are not BN-specific Mendelian causes.

evidence.snippet: Cognitive behavioral therapy reduces core behavioral and psychological features in the short and long term.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review supports CBT efficacy.

evidence.snippet: follow by addressing the eating disorder psychopathology (for example, the extreme dietary restraint, the concerns about body shape and weight, and the tendency to binge eat in response to difficult thoughts and feelings)
evidence.explanation: Specifies CBT targets.

evidence.snippet: Do not offer medication as the sole treatment for bulimia nervosa.
evidence.explanation: Psychological care remains central.

treatments/0.description: CBT addresses regular eating, rigid dietary rules, overvaluation of shape and weight, emotional triggers and relapse prevention. NICE recommends individual CBT when guided self-help is unsuitable or ineffective; APA recommends eating-disorder-focused CBT for adults together with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Medication should not be the sole treatment.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: CBT addresses rigid eating rules and shape/weight concerns.

treatments/0/targets/1.description: CBT develops responses to difficult thoughts and feelings that can trigger binge eating.

evidence.snippet: Consider bulimia-nervosa-focused guided self-help for adults with bulimia nervosa.
evidence.explanation: Adult guided self-help recommendation.

evidence.snippet: use cognitive behavioural self-help materials for eating disorders
evidence.explanation: Specifies the intervention content.

treatments/1.description: NICE advises considering BN-focused guided self-help for adults, using structured cognitive behavioral materials with brief supportive sessions. Assess response and consider individual CBT if it is unacceptable, contraindicated or ineffective after four weeks.

evidence.snippet: use a collaborative approach between the parents and the young person to establish regular eating patterns and minimise compensatory behaviours
evidence.explanation: Family involvement is collaborative, not an assertion of family causation.

evidence.snippet: Participants in FBT-BN achieved higher abstinence rates than in CBT-A at end of treatment (39% versus 20%; p = .040, number needed to treat [NNT] = 5) and at 6-month follow-up (44% versus 25%; p = .030, NNT = 5).
evidence.explanation: Randomized comparison; full text identifies 109 participants in these two arms of a three-arm study.

evidence.snippet: Abstinence rates between these 2 groups did not differ statistically at 12-month follow-up
evidence.explanation: The longer follow-up does not establish sustained comparative superiority.

treatments/2.description: Family-based treatment collaboratively supports regular eating and reduction of compensatory behaviors without blaming families. In a randomized trial of adolescents with full or partial BN, FBT-BN yielded higher abstinence than adolescent CBT at end of treatment and six months, but the difference was not significant at twelve months. Missing follow-up and specialized settings limit generalization. Individual CBT is an alternative when family treatment is unsuitable or ineffective.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Family-supported behavior change aims to reduce compensation.

treatments/2/targets/1.description: Supported regular eating aims to interrupt recurrent binge episodes.

evidence.snippet: Fluoxetine at 60 mg/d proved superior to placebo in decreasing the frequency of weekly binge-eating and vomiting episodes at end point.
evidence.explanation: Eight-week randomized trial of 387 outpatient women, comparing 60 mg, 20 mg and placebo.

evidence.snippet: either initially or if there is minimal or no response to psychotherapy alone by 6 weeks of treatment.
evidence.explanation: The final APA 2023 recommendation combines medication with eating-disorder-focused CBT.

evidence.snippet: Several adverse events (ie, insomnia, nausea, asthenia, and tremor) occurred significantly more frequently with fluoxetine (60 or 20 mg/d) than with placebo.
evidence.explanation: Trial adverse effects; discontinuation due to adverse events did not differ significantly.

treatments/3.description: Fluoxetine 60 mg/day has placebo-controlled evidence for reducing binge and vomiting frequency in adults. APA recommends a serotonin reuptake inhibitor with CBT initially or after minimal response to psychotherapy by six weeks. Treatment response does not demonstrate a primary serotonin deficiency. Insomnia, nausea, asthenia and tremor occurred more often than with placebo in the founding trial.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Fluoxetine can reduce binge frequency; the disease-level molecular mechanism remains uncertain.

treatments/3/targets/1.description: Randomized evidence supports reduced vomiting frequency.

evidence.snippet: The primary efficacy measure, mean weekly number of binge and/or purge days, decreased 44.8% from baseline with topiramate versus 10.7% with placebo (p =.004).
evidence.explanation: Ten-week randomized trial; this is change in days, not a remission rate.

evidence.snippet: Despite the published evidence, olanzapine and topiramate have not received marketing authorisation for use in EDs from any medicine regulatory agency.
evidence.explanation: Guideline separates evidence from regulatory authorization.

treatments/4.description: Topiramate has randomized short-term efficacy evidence and is recommended in the 2023 WFSBP pharmacological guideline, but has no eating-disorder marketing authorization. In a 69-person trial with 64 included in the intention-to-treat analysis, weekly binge/purge days decreased more than with placebo; not every secondary endpoint was significant. Specialist assessment of tolerability and individual risks is required.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Short-term trial evidence supports reduction in binge/purge days.

evidence.snippet: Provide acute medical care (including emergency admission) for people with an eating disorder who have severe electrolyte imbalance, severe malnutrition, severe dehydration or signs of incipient organ failure.
evidence.explanation: Defines acute escalation indications.

evidence.snippet: For people with an eating disorder who need supplements to restore electrolyte balance, offer these orally unless the person has problems with gastrointestinal absorption or the electrolyte disturbance is severe.
evidence.explanation: Replacement route depends on clinical severity.

evidence.snippet: we demonstrate that SARS-CoV-2 uses the SARS-CoV receptor ACE2 for entry and the serine protease TMPRSS2 for S protein priming
evidence.explanation: Hoffmann et al. directly establish the ACE2 receptor and TMPRSS2-priming entry mechanism that defines SARS-CoV-2 cell tropism.

steps/2.description: SARS-CoV-2 enters host cells via its spike (S) glycoprotein binding the cellular receptor ACE2, followed by S protein priming by the host serine protease TMPRSS2. ACE2 and TMPRSS2 co-expression on nasal, conducting airway, and alveolar epithelial cells (particularly ciliated cells and type II pneumocytes) defines the principal cellular tropism that drives upper- and lower-respiratory disease.

evidence.snippet: After viral entry, two overlapping polyproteins, pp1a (490 kDa) and pp1ab (794 kDa), are translated by the translational machinery of the host.
evidence.explanation: The structural study explicitly identifies host translation of pp1a and pp1ab as the precursor-producing step after viral entry.

steps/3.description: Following entry and release of the positive-sense RNA genome, host translational machinery produces the overlapping SARS-CoV-2 replicase polyproteins pp1a and pp1ab. These precursors contain the nonstructural proteins that must be released by PLpro and Mpro cleavage before the viral replication machinery is functional.

evidence.snippet: Mpro is a cysteine protease that cleaves at no less than 11 sites on the replicase polyproteins
evidence.explanation: The structural study directly defines Mpro's catalytic role and cleavage burden on the SARS-CoV-2 replicase polyproteins.

evidence.snippet: Mpro of SARS-CoV-2 digests replicase polyproteins, releasing the nonstructural proteins (nsps)
evidence.explanation: This directly supports release of nonstructural proteins as the output of the Mpro processing step.

steps/4.description: SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro, also called 3CLpro or nsp5) is the viral cysteine protease that cleaves at least 11 sites in the replicase polyproteins pp1a and pp1ab. This releases nonstructural proteins needed for the replication-transcription machinery. Mpro is distinct from the viral papain-like protease PLpro, which performs other cleavage events.

evidence.snippet: activation of the IFN response induces ADP-ribosylation of host proteins
evidence.explanation: Russo et al. show that interferon-response activation drives host protein ADP-ribosylation, instantiating the IFN-PARP arm of the macrodomain module in human cells exposed to SARS-CoV-2 Nsp3.

steps/5.description: SARS-CoV-2 replication is sensed by pattern-recognition receptors that induce type I and type III interferon signaling in infected respiratory epithelium. Interferon signaling drives expression of PARP family members (including PARP9 paired with the DTX3L E3 ligase) that catalyze antiviral ADP-ribosylation as part of the innate antiviral program.

evidence.snippet: replicase polyproteins essential for viral replication and transcription
evidence.explanation: The study ties the Mpro-processed replicase polyproteins to viral replication and transcription.

steps/6.description: Processed SARS-CoV-2 nonstructural proteins, including the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and helicase, form and support the replication-transcription machinery that copies viral RNA. This is the replicase-branch output of polyprotein processing and the downstream process interrupted by nirmatrelvir inhibition of Mpro.

evidence.snippet: This IFN-induced ADP-ribosylation is dependent on PARP9 and its binding partner DTX3L
evidence.explanation: Russo et al. identify PARP9/DTX3L as the IFN-dependent ADP-ribosylation machinery whose product the Nsp3 macrodomain reverses.

steps/7.description: The interferon-inducible PARP9 ADP-ribosyltransferase, in complex with the DTX3L E3 ligase, mono-ADP-ribosylates host proteins as a downstream effector of the host antiviral interferon response. This NAD-dependent modification is the substrate that the SARS-CoV-2 Nsp3 macrodomain targets and reverses.

evidence.snippet: All coronaviruses encode a highly conserved macrodomain (Mac1) that binds to and removes ADP-ribose adducts from proteins
evidence.explanation: Alhammad et al. directly establish that the SARS-CoV-2 Mac1 macrodomain is a conserved ADP-ribose hydrolase, the defining viral countermeasure enzyme.

evidence.snippet: Mac1 is essential for pathogenesis in multiple animal models of CoV infection
evidence.explanation: Mac1's essentiality across multiple in vivo coronavirus infection models supports the macrodomain as the obligate viral pivot for ADP-ribosylation countermeasure rather than an accessory function.

evidence.snippet: ectopic expression of the SARS-CoV-2 Nsp3 macrodomain reverses this modification in human cells
evidence.explanation: Russo et al. directly demonstrate Nsp3 macrodomain-mediated reversal of PARP9/DTX3L-deposited ADP-ribosylation in human cells.

evidence.snippet: the cellular function of the SARS-CoV-2 Nsp3 macrodomain is to hydrolyze this end product of IFN signaling, rather than to suppress the IFN response itself
evidence.explanation: The macrodomain acts at the effector level of the IFN antiviral program (the ADP-ribosylated end product), not at upstream IFN signaling — the interactome-rebalancing framing under which Mac1 is a precision pivot.

evidence.snippet: However, in a mouse model of severe infection, ΔMac1 was quickly cleared causing minimal pathology without any morbidity. ΔMac1 SARS-CoV-2 induced increased levels of interferon (IFN) and IFN-stimulated gene expression in cell culture and mice, indicating that Mac1 blocks IFN responses which may contribute to its attenuation.
evidence.explanation: Reverse genetics in SARS-CoV-2 itself, rather than in a surrogate coronavirus: complete deletion of the macrodomain leaves replication near wild type in cell lines but abolishes pathogenesis in mice, with a heightened interferon and interferon-stimulated gene response. This is the direct genetic demonstration that the node's function is immune counteraction rather than replication support.

evidence.snippet: We identified interactions between Mac1 and ADP-ribosylated substrates involved in DNA damage response, cytoskeletal components, and cell cycle regulation.
evidence.explanation: Affinity proteomics comparing wild-type Mac1 with the catalytically dead N40D mutant places candidate ADP-ribosylated clients outside interferon signaling, including TRiC chaperonin subunits in lung-derived A549 cells. Two limits: the experiment transfects an isolated Strep-tagged Mac1 domain rather than infecting cells, and the paper presents these as putative clients awaiting functional validation, so this widens the candidate substrate set without redefining the node's established interferon-directed function.

steps/8.description: SARS-CoV-2 encodes a conserved macrodomain (Mac1) within nonstructural protein 3 (Nsp3) that binds and hydrolyzes mono-ADP-ribose marks on host proteins. Mac1 reverses the PARP9/DTX3L-dependent antiviral ADP-ribosylation that the host interferon response deposits, neutralizing this branch of innate immunity. The macrodomain is essential for coronavirus pathogenesis in animal models and is the prototypical viral pivot point for this mechanism module. Its conserved fold and druggable ADP-ribose pocket make it an attractive target for both small-molecule inhibitors and PROTAC-style degraders.

evidence.snippet: The macrodomain is essential for CoV pathogenesis and may be a novel therapeutic target.
evidence.explanation: Macrodomain essentiality for coronavirus pathogenesis links the Mac1 activity directly to viral replication and tissue pathology in vivo.

steps/9.description: By neutralizing host PARP9/DTX3L-dependent antiviral ADP-ribosylation, the Nsp3 macrodomain permits sustained viral replication in respiratory epithelium, leading to alveolar epithelial injury, diffuse alveolar damage, and recruitment of innate immune effectors. The interplay of viral cytopathic injury and dysregulated host responses drives the pneumonia, hypoxemia, and acute respiratory distress syndrome that characterize severe COVID-19.

evidence.snippet: Compared with non-ICU patients, ICU patients had higher plasma levels of IL2, IL7, IL10, GSCF, IP10, MCP1, MIP1A, and TNFα.
evidence.explanation: Huang et al. directly document the hyperinflammatory cytokine profile that distinguishes severe ICU-level COVID-19 from milder disease.

evidence.snippet: Complications included acute respiratory distress syndrome
evidence.explanation: The Wuhan cohort directly links severe COVID-19 to ARDS as the dominant lethal complication.

steps/10.description: A subset of patients develops severe lower-respiratory disease with elevated inflammatory cytokines, lymphopenia, diffuse alveolar damage, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Markedly elevated IL-6 and other inflammatory mediators identify a hyperinflammatory state amenable to corticosteroid and anti-cytokine therapy.

evidence.snippet: Such complex manifestations suggest that SARS-CoV-2 dysregulates the host response, triggering wide-ranging immuno-inflammatory, thrombotic, and parenchymal derangements.
evidence.explanation: Osuchowski et al. frame severe COVID-19 as a host-response dysregulation producing immuno-inflammatory and thrombotic derangements — the endotheliopathy-centred pathophysiology this node captures.

evidence.snippet: d-dimer greater than 1 μg/mL (18·42, 2·64-128·55; p=0·0033)
evidence.explanation: Admission D-dimer greater than 1 μg/mL is a strong independent mortality risk factor, the clinical readout of the prothrombotic coagulopathy modeled by this node.

evidence.snippet: the COVID-19 group had higher smoking rates, STEMI (50% vs. 26.3%), and elevated D-dimer, C reactive protein (CRP), and cardiac troponins. COVID-19 patients had more ventricular thrombus (15% vs. 3.75%), RV dilation (36.25% vs. 11.25%), and pulmonary hypertension (50% vs. 26.3%)
evidence.explanation: Riyadh (King Saud Medical City) case-control angiographic study directly demonstrates COVID-19-driven prothrombotic coagulopathy with cardiac-specific manifestations: elevated D-dimer, ventricular thrombus, and elevated troponins document endothelial injury and thrombotic complications; pulmonary hypertension and RV dilation extend the endotheliopathy model to pulmonary vasculature.

steps/11.description: Beyond direct respiratory epithelial injury, severe COVID-19 is characterized by endothelial activation and a prothrombotic coagulopathy. SARS-CoV-2-driven immuno-inflammatory and endothelial derangements promote micro- and macro-vascular thrombosis — reflected clinically in elevated D-dimer — and contribute to the multi-organ dysfunction that defines the lethal disease phenotype. This node instantiates the emerging endotheliopathy-centred pathophysiology model at the tissue scale, parallel to the cellular macrodomain immune-evasion arm.

evidence.explanation: TMPRSS2 priming is a druggable host-directed step in SARS-CoV-2 entry.

genes/1.notes: TMPRSS2 is the principal host serine protease that primes the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein for membrane fusion. Pharmacologic inhibition of TMPRSS2 blocks viral entry in cell culture and is a validated host-directed antiviral strategy.

evidence.explanation: The 2025 IDSA guideline update recommends nirmatrelvir/ritonavir among the antivirals for mild-to-moderate COVID-19 in adults.

treatments/0.description: Oral nirmatrelvir directly inhibits SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro/3CLpro), while ritonavir inhibits host CYP3A to increase nirmatrelvir exposure rather than serving as a second SARS-CoV-2 protease inhibitor. The regimen is recommended for outpatients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 at high risk of progression to severe disease.

evidence.snippet: discovery and characterization of PF-07321332, an orally bioavailable SARS-CoV-2 main protease inhibitor with in vitro pan-human coronavirus antiviral activity
evidence.explanation: PF-07321332 is nirmatrelvir; the primary discovery study directly identifies it as a SARS-CoV-2 main-protease inhibitor with antiviral activity.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: The nirmatrelvir component directly inhibits SARS-CoV-2 Mpro and thereby blocks Mpro-dependent processing of pp1a and pp1ab. Ritonavir's role in this regimen is pharmacokinetic enhancement through host CYP3A inhibition, separate from this viral target edge.

evidence.snippet: The guideline panel presents 9 updated recommendations on the use of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, remdesivir, and molnupiravir, in adults with mild to moderate COVID-19.
evidence.explanation: The 2025 IDSA guideline update includes remdesivir among the recommended antivirals for mild-to-moderate COVID-19.

treatments/1.description: Intravenous nucleotide-analog inhibitor of the SARS-CoV-2 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, used in hospitalized patients with COVID-19 requiring supplemental oxygen.

treatments/2.description: Systemic corticosteroid that reduces mortality in patients with COVID-19 requiring supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation by suppressing the hyperinflammatory host response.

treatments/3.description: Active immunization against the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (mRNA, adenoviral vector, recombinant protein, and inactivated platforms) is the principal population-level intervention against COVID-19 and reduces severe disease and death.

treatments/4.description: Pegylated interferon lambda-1A is an innate-immunity-modulator (a type III interferon) that pharmacologically augments the host interferon-stimulated antiviral state. In the TOGETHER randomized trial, a single subcutaneous dose given early to outpatients significantly reduced COVID-19 hospitalization or emergency-department visits, with benefit consistent across SARS-CoV-2 variants — the broad-spectrum, host-directed signature of an interferon-based antiviral.

evidence.snippet: Among predominantly vaccinated outpatients with Covid-19, the incidence of hospitalization or an emergency department visit (observation for >6 hours) was significantly lower among those who received a single dose of pegylated interferon lambda than among those who received placebo.
evidence.explanation: Randomized-trial evidence that augmenting the interferon response with peginterferon lambda restricts COVID-19, supporting this treatment's action on the interferon node. Evidence source is HUMAN_CLINICAL as this is a randomized controlled trial.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Peginterferon lambda supplies exogenous type III interferon that reinforces the host interferon-stimulated antiviral program this node initiates, restricting viral replication; it conceptually counters the viral macrodomain countermeasure that degrades the downstream ADP-ribosylation output.

evidence.snippet: Mac1 is essential for pathogenesis in multiple animal models of CoV infection
evidence.explanation: In vivo essentiality across multiple coronavirus models directly supports the canonical Mac1 essentiality hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: the cellular function of the SARS-CoV-2 Nsp3 macrodomain is to hydrolyze this end product of IFN signaling, rather than to suppress the IFN response itself
evidence.explanation: Russo et al. position Mac1 at the effector end of the IFN antiviral cascade, consistent with the canonical countermeasure model.

hypotheses/0.description: The SARS-CoV-2 Nsp3 macrodomain (Mac1) is a conserved coronavirus mono-ADP-ribosylhydrolase that is essential for pathogenesis. By hydrolyzing PARP9/DTX3L-deposited mono-ADP-ribose marks on host proteins, Mac1 neutralizes the effector branch of the host interferon antiviral program and is required for productive replication in vivo. This is the disease-level instantiation of the parp_parg_macrodomain_viral_evasion module's canonical countermeasure hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: evidence for many distinctive mechanistic features indicates that COVID-19 constitutes a new disease entity, with emerging data suggesting involvement of an endotheliopathy-centred pathophysiology
evidence.explanation: Osuchowski et al. Lancet Respir Med review positions endotheliopathy as the unifying pathophysiological framework for severe COVID-19, distinct from purely respiratory cytopathic injury.

evidence.snippet: Such complex manifestations suggest that SARS-CoV-2 dysregulates the host response, triggering wide-ranging immuno-inflammatory, thrombotic, and parenchymal derangements.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the multi-system, interactome-rebalancing framing of severe COVID-19 as a host-response dysregulation rather than direct viral cytopathology alone.

hypotheses/1.description: Severe COVID-19 is increasingly framed as an endotheliopathy in which SARS-CoV-2-driven endothelial activation, thrombo-inflammation, and parenchymal injury — rather than direct cytopathic respiratory infection alone — define the lethal disease phenotype. Under the interactome-rebalancing framing, the lung endothelial interactome shifts toward a pro-thrombotic, hyper-inflammatory state that sits downstream of viral entry but upstream of multi-organ dysfunction. This hypothesis is parallel to (not subsumed by) the macrodomain countermeasure model: Mac1 explains immune evasion at the cellular level, while endotheliopathy explains organ-scale pathology and many of the distinctive thrombotic complications.

evidence.snippet: SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV, and Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) Mac1 domains exhibit similar structural folds, and all 3 proteins bound to ADP-ribose with affinities in the low micromolar range
evidence.explanation: Structural conservation of Mac1 across coronaviruses supports the feasibility of a pan-CoV pivot-control strategy beyond active-site inhibition.

evidence.snippet: Significant efforts have been recently dedicated to the discovery of small molecule inhibitors against the Macrodomain 1 (Mac1) of nonstructural protein 3 (NSP3) as potential antivirals for SARS-CoV-2.
evidence.explanation: Ban et al. and the CACHE3 challenge directly demonstrate that Mac1 is an active drug-discovery target with community-wide investment, supporting the feasibility of allosteric and PROTAC-warhead programs.

evidence.snippet: Our results illustrate the effectiveness of ML-accelerated docking to rapidly identify novel chemical series and provide a strong foundation for the development of SARS-CoV-2 NSP3 Mac1 inhibitors.
evidence.explanation: The community-level chemistry infrastructure for Mac1 hit-finding lowers the experimental barrier for the proposed Mac1 conformational pivot experiment.

evidence.snippet: Despite increased ADP-ribose binding, I-A mutant MERS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 were highly attenuated in both cell culture and mice, indicating that this isoleucine residue acts as a gate that controls ADP-ribose binding for efficient virus replication.
evidence.explanation: Kerr et al. provide the strongest direct support for the conformational-pivot framing: a GIF-motif I-A mutation that enhances substrate binding without impairing catalysis still attenuates the virus in vivo, demonstrating that Mac1's conformational landscape (not just enzymatic output) is critical for viral fitness. Stabilizing an unproductive conformation could therefore achieve antiviral effects beyond what active-site inhibition alone provides.

evidence.snippet: Overall, 160 ligands in 119 different scaffolds were discovered, and 153 Mac1-ligand complex crystal structures were determined, typically to 1 Å resolution or better.
evidence.explanation: Gahbauer et al. provide the largest crystallographic dataset for any macrodomain. The diversity of scaffolds and the observed ligand-mediated conformational changes establish Mac1 as a conformationally plastic target amenable to allosteric and conformational-state-selective chemistry.

evidence.snippet: Our analyses discovered selective and cell-permeable molecules, unexpected ligand-mediated conformational changes within the active site
evidence.explanation: Observed conformational plasticity in response to diverse ligands directly supports the assumption that Mac1 can be addressed by conformational-state-selective chemistry, not only orthosteric inhibition.

evidence.snippet: we identified a selective, allosteric and cell-active macrodomain inhibitor, GeA-69, targeting macrodomain 2 of PARP14 in vitro and in intact cells where it prevents its localisation to the sites of DNA damage.
evidence.explanation: Schuller et al. provide the validated allosteric precedent for any macrodomain protein. GeA-69 binds outside the ADP-ribose pocket yet blocks PARP14 MD2 function in cells, demonstrating that macrodomain allosteric chemistry is feasible and can achieve selectivity advantages over orthosteric approaches. This is the closest direct precedent for the proposed Mac1 allosteric pivot strategy.

evidence.snippet: Following infection, D1329A displayed a large defect in the accumulation of viral RNA compared to WT or N1347A in all cells tested. Alternatively, N1347A infection produced normal levels of viral RNA but produced reduced levels of viral protein in interferon-competent bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs).
evidence.explanation: In mouse hepatitis virus strain JHM, an adenine-binding mutation and a hydrolysis mutation impair different stages of the replication cycle. Mac1 is therefore not a single-activity enzyme whose output can be fully described by catalytic rate, which is the substantive basis for treating it as a conformational pivot rather than only as a hydrolase active site.

evidence.snippet: Expression studies of the macrodomain-PLP2 portion of nsp3 indicate that the ts mutations enhance proteasome-mediated degradation of the protein.
evidence.explanation: Destabilizing the macrodomain routes the expressed macrodomain-PLP2 region of nsp3 into proteasomal degradation, which is the closest published analogue of the degradation arm of this hypothesis. Two limits on how far it can be carried: the work is in mouse hepatitis virus, and the construct is a macrodomain-PLP2 fragment rather than full-length nsp3, so it does not establish that a Mac1-directed warhead would degrade the intact membrane-associated polyprotein.

evidence.snippet: inhibition of nsp3-mac1 increases ADP-ribosylation, but surprisingly does not translate to demonstrable antiviral activity in cell culture and iPSC-derived pneumocyte models
evidence.explanation: Low-nanomolar orthosteric inhibitors engaged the target and raised ADP-ribosylation without producing antiviral activity, including in combination with interferon gamma. This is the strongest published case that active-site occupancy alone may not be sufficient, which is the premise the conformational-pivot framing rests on. Whether the null result reflects the compounds or the assay system remains unsettled.

evidence.snippet: In an animal model of severe SARS-CoV-2 infection, AVI-4206 reduces viral replication, potentiates innate immune responses, and leads to a survival benefit.
evidence.explanation: Refutes the hypothesis's premise that broad antiviral effect is something "active-site inhibition alone may not achieve". A conventional ADP-ribose-pocket inhibitor delivers pharmacological proof of concept in vivo, including a survival benefit. An allosteric or degradation-based strategy must now demonstrate added value in breadth, resistance profile or potency rather than merely working.

evidence.snippet: While active molecules discovered by CACHE #3 participants largely mimicked the adenine ring of the endogenous substrate, ADP-ribose, preserving the canonical chemotype commonly observed in previously reported Nsp3-Mac1 ligands
evidence.explanation: Refutes the specific sub-claim that the third CACHE challenge supplies a starting point for conformational-pivot chemistry. Twenty-three groups selecting 1739 candidates converged on canonical adenine-mimetic orthosteric ligands and produced no allosteric series, so CACHE #3 establishes target tractability without supplying the non-orthosteric chemical matter this hypothesis requires.

hypotheses/2.description: The conserved Mac1 fold across coronaviruses (SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV) supports treating Mac1 as a thermodynamic pivot point rather than only an active-site target. Allosteric stabilization of distinct Mac1 conformational states or PROTAC-based physical degradation would rebalance the host interactome toward antiviral ADP-ribosylation, with potential broad anti-coronavirus activity that active-site inhibition alone may not achieve. Active drug-discovery programs (including the third CACHE community challenge) have established Mac1 as a tractable structural target with hundreds of crystallographically characterized ligands, providing a strong starting point for conformational-pivot chemistry.

evidence.snippet: stress- and treatment-induced hyperglycaemia is common in critical illness, occurring in approximately 50% of affected individuals. While often transient, these effects may unmask persistent metabolic dysfunction in individuals at risk of type 2 diabetes [36, 37].
evidence.explanation: Identifies the unresolved distinction: acute hyperglycemia may be reversible stress-response versus a marker of persistent damage.

open_questions/0.rationale: COVID-19 hospitalized patients frequently develop hyperglycemia (~50%), but the majority resolve it post-discharge. However, population cohort studies (OpenSAFELY, N3C) and registry data report incident diabetes cases years post-infection. The mechanism(s) linking acute infection-driven hyperglycemia to persistent diabetes risk is not clear: stress-hyperglycemia may unmask pre-existing insulin resistance that progresses to type 2 diabetes, acute direct infection of beta cells may cause lasting damage, or unresolved post-viral inflammation may sustain pathways months/years later. A prospective multi-timepoint mechanistic study is needed.

evidence.snippet: Soon, additional studies began to identify similar increases in new-onset type 2 diabetes [17].
evidence.explanation: Documents both type 1 and type 2 incidence increases post-COVID, raising the question of shared versus divergent mechanisms.

open_questions/1.rationale: Meta-analyses and prospective cohorts report increased incidence of both type 1 diabetes (especially in children with new-onset DKA above baseline) and type 2 diabetes (particularly in hospitalized and older adults). The role of SARS-CoV-2 as a direct trigger of autoimmunity, a driver of insulin resistance through persistent inflammation, or an unmasker of pre-existing glucose intolerance is not yet resolved. Mechanistic and genetic factors that predict which type develops are largely unknown.

evidence.snippet: Recombinant virus with these mutations had enhanced replication compared with the WT virus when treated with 5a, demonstrating the specificity of these compounds during infection. However, this virus is highly attenuated in vivo, indicating that drug resistance emerged at the expense of viral fitness.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the resistance baseline this gap must be measured against. Escape from an active-site Mac1 inhibitor is achievable by serial passage but costs viral fitness, so any claim that conformational or degradation-based control offers a resistance advantage now has a concrete comparator rather than an empty field.

evidence.snippet: Twenty-three groups deployed diverse design strategies to collectively select 1739 ligand candidates. While over 85% of the designed molecules were chemically novel, the best experimentally confirmed hits were structurally similar to previously published compounds.
evidence.explanation: A community-scale hit-finding effort against Mac1 recovered the known orthosteric chemotype, which is why the absence of a non-orthosteric chemical starting point is recorded here as a knowledge gap rather than as a gap in effort.

open_questions/2.rationale:
The Nsp3 Mac1 macrodomain is a conserved, structurally tractable viral enzyme that selectively hydrolyzes the end product of the host IFN-PARP antiviral program. Active-site inhibitors target the ADP-ribose pocket directly, but the broader interactome framing suggests an alternative: stabilize defined conformational states of Mac1 with allosteric binders to test how each conformation reshapes the host PARP-mediated antiviral response, or eliminate the protein outright with a viral-protein-directed PROTAC warhead. Because Mac1 folds are conserved across SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV, and MERS-CoV, conformational stabilizers or degraders may have broad anti-coronavirus activity — the kind of pivot-point control that distinguishes a thermodynamic interactome framing from single-enzyme inhibition.
Both arms of the question are open at the level of chemical matter, not merely of biology. No allosteric site has been identified or characterized on any viral macrodomain; the only validated macrodomain allosteric ligand series remains GeA-69 against human PARP14 macrodomain 2, whose selectivity derives from PARP14-specific features. No Mac1-directed PROTAC has been designed, synthesized, or tested, and every published SARS-CoV-2 degrader targets a standalone viral protein rather than a domain embedded in the membrane-associated nsp3 polyprotein. The third CACHE challenge screened 1739 candidate ligands from 23 groups and returned only canonical adenine-mimetic orthosteric chemotypes, so community hit-finding has not yet produced a non-orthosteric starting point either.
The comparator arm has meanwhile moved. Active-site inhibition now has in vivo pharmacological proof of concept (AVI-4206) and an independent chemotype that represses coronavirus replication, and serial passage under that second chemotype has already produced a resistant Mac1 double mutant that is itself attenuated in mice. Allosteric or degradation-based control therefore has to demonstrate specific added value in breadth, resistance profile, or efficacy, not merely that it works.

evidence.snippet: identifying inborn errors of type I interferon (IFN) immunity in 1-5% of unvaccinated patients with critical pneumonia, and their autoimmune phenocopy, autoantibodies against type I IFN, in another 15-20% of cases
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the patient fraction in whom the host arm of the Mac1 therapeutic mechanism is already compromised, which is what makes the efficacy question a real stratification problem rather than a theoretical caveat.

evidence.snippet: Standard cellular models indicate that AVI-4206 has high target engagement and can weakly inhibit viral replication in a gamma interferon- and Mac1 catalytic activity-dependent manner.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the dependence itself: target engagement alone does not produce antiviral activity, and the effect requires both interferon signaling and Mac1 catalysis. This is the mechanistic reason to expect reduced benefit in interferon-deficient patients.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, 5c and 6e inhibited SARS-CoV-2 replication only in the presence of IFN
evidence.explanation: An independent chemical series reproduces the same interferon dependence, so the constraint is a property of Mac1 inhibition rather than of one compound.

open_questions/3.rationale:
Every published Mac1 inhibitor whose mechanism has been dissected acts through immune restoration rather than through direct antiviral blockade, and in both compound series the cellular antiviral effect is explicitly interferon dependent. That makes host interferon competence a gate on the entire therapeutic strategy, and the gate is not hypothetical: inborn errors of type I interferon immunity account for 1 to 5 percent of unvaccinated patients with critical pneumonia and anti-interferon autoantibodies for another 15 to 20 percent, so the patients most likely to need a novel antiviral are enriched for the defect that would blunt it.
The gap is that this has never been tested. No Mac1 inhibitor has entered a clinical trial, so no cohort stratified by interferon autoantibody status or by interferon-stimulated gene score exists, and the preclinical interferon dependence has only been shown by adding or withholding interferon gamma in culture, not by comparing hosts that differ in endogenous type I interferon capacity. Resolving it needs either an animal model with defined type I interferon pathway loss treated with an active-site Mac1 inhibitor, or prospective collection of anti-interferon autoantibody status in any future trial. The answer bears directly on the Mac1 pivot hypothesis's claim of broad activity, because the limitation applies equally to active-site, allosteric, and degradation-based approaches.

evidence.snippet: We summarise proposed pathophysiological mechanisms, including the effects of SARS-CoV-2 infection in the pancreas and on peripheral insulin-sensitive tissues. We review key meta-analyses assessing the association between COVID-19 and incident type 1 and type 2 diabetes and highlight strengths and weaknesses of the epidemiologic studies
evidence.explanation: Said et al. identify this mechanistic gap as a critical uncertainty, noting conflicting evidence on direct pancreatic tropism vs. systemic inflammation as drivers of acute hyperglycemia and post-COVID diabetes.

open_questions/4.rationale: Post-acute SARS-CoV-2 infection has been associated with new-onset diabetes, raising the mechanistic question of direct viral pancreatic tropism vs. systemic inflammation as the driver. A comprehensive post-pandemic review (Said et al. 2026, Diabetologia) identifies conflicting evidence on whether SARS-CoV-2 directly infects pancreatic beta cells during acute infection, or whether acute hyperglycemia and persistent metabolic dysfunction post-COVID result from HPA-axis stress, pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-6, IL-1beta), and reduced peripheral insulin sensitivity. This distinction is mechanistically consequential: direct beta-cell tropism could produce permanent damage and predict Type 1-like post-COVID diabetes, whereas inflammation-mediated dysfunction would predict reversible Type 2 hyperglycemia. Resolution of this branch informs the mechanistic link to post-COVID diabetes development modeled in Long_COVID entry.

evidence.snippet: Crumbs homolog 1-A is primarily expressed in Müller cells and plays a vital role in retinal development, whereas CRB1-B, expressed in photoreceptors, helps maintain long-term retinal integrity in adult retinas.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the cell-type assignment of the two isoforms and their differing developmental versus maintenance roles.

evidence.snippet: CRB1-A is localized to the apical tips of Müller cells and CRB1-B in the inner and outer segments with a gradient
evidence.explanation: Gives the subcellular localisation of each isoform, on either side of the outer limiting membrane.

evidence.snippet: CRB1-A is the predominant isoform during developmental stages. By contrast, CRB1-B is by far the most abundant isoform in the adult human, as well as murine retina.
evidence.explanation: Supports the developmental versus adult division of labour between the two isoforms.

evidence.snippet: All patients had variants affecting CRB1-A, with none exclusively affecting CRB1-B.
evidence.explanation: Across 389 patients from 50 cohorts, CRB1-A involvement was universal, supporting it as a necessary condition for disease.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in exons 6, 7, and 9 were associated to LCA/EOSRD and RP phenotypes, whereas exon 2 variants were linked to MD.
evidence.explanation: Shows that exon position, which determines isoform involvement, tracks with the clinical phenotype.

steps/1.description: CRB1 is transcribed in the retina as two major isoforms occupying different cells. The canonical 12-exon CRB1-A is expressed in Muller glia and is the predominant isoform during retinal development; the shorter CRB1-B is expressed in photoreceptors and is the more abundant isoform in the adult retina. Both reach the outer limiting membrane from opposite sides of the same junction. Because a variant's exon position determines which transcripts it disrupts, one gene produces cell-type-partitioned lesions rather than a single uniform loss: exon 6, 7 and 9 variants hit both isoforms, whereas exon 2 variants such as c.498_506del p.(Ile167_Gly169del) affect CRB1-A only and leave CRB1-B intact. In the largest genotype series assembled to date every patient carried a variant affecting CRB1-A and none was CRB1-B-exclusive, so CRB1-A involvement appears necessary for disease.

evidence.snippet: Shortened photoreceptor inner and outer segments are observed as early as 2 weeks after birth, suggesting a developmental defect in these structures rather than a degenerative process.
evidence.explanation: The rd8 mouse model demonstrates that CRB1 is essential for photoreceptor morphogenesis and OLM integrity.

evidence.snippet: CRB1 consists of 12 exons and exhibits alternative splicing at the 3' end, yielding two proteins of 1376 and 1406 amino acids
evidence.explanation: This review describes CRB1 protein structure including transmembrane and cytoplasmic domains critical for junction formation.

steps/2.description: CRB1 localizes to the apical membrane of photoreceptors and Muller glial cells at the outer limiting membrane (OLM), where it maintains adherens junction integrity and cell polarity. Biallelic loss-of-function variants disrupt this structural scaffold, creating the shared proximal defect across the CRB1 disease family.

evidence.snippet: Photoreceptor degeneration is observed only within regions of retinal spotting, which is seen predominantly in the inferior nasal quadrant of the eye, and is caused by retinal folds and pseudorosettes.
evidence.explanation: Mouse model shows retinal disorganization with folds and pseudorosettes preceding degeneration.

evidence.snippet: The poor OCT lamination may have a degenerative component, as well as being congenital.
evidence.explanation: Clinical imaging suggests both developmental and degenerative contributions to retinal disorganization.

steps/3.description: Disrupted OLM integrity leads to abnormal retinal lamination with a thickened, immature-appearing retina. This structural disorganization affects both photoreceptor and Muller cell architecture and may have both developmental (congenital) and degenerative components.

evidence.snippet: Severe visual impairment was most frequent after 40 years of age for patients with RP and after 20 years of age for EOSRD/LCA.
evidence.explanation: Documents the differential timeline of severe visual impairment across CRB1 subtypes.

evidence.snippet: In the RP group, median ages for reaching low vision, severe visual impairment, and blindness were 18, 32, and 44 years, respectively, with a visual acuity decline rate of 0.03 logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution per year.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the progressive visual loss trajectory in CRB1-RP patients.

evidence.snippet: Microperimetry showed a significant decrease in retinal sensitivity during follow-up and may be a more sensitive progression marker.
evidence.explanation: Prospective natural history data confirms ongoing retinal sensitivity decline in CRB1 patients.

steps/4.description: End-stage convergence across subtypes involves progressive rod and cone loss with declining visual acuity, visual field constriction, and extinguished electroretinogram. The rate of progression varies by subtype, with LCA/EOSRD showing earlier severe impairment than RP, and visual acuity survival analyses indicating an optimal intervention window in the first 2-3 decades.

evidence.snippet: Night blindness was present in all patients but three, for whom a decrease of central vision and photophobia dominated.
evidence.explanation: Night blindness was present in the majority of CRB1-RP patients in this French cohort.

steps/5.description: Night blindness is a common presenting symptom in the RP branch, reflecting early rod photoreceptor dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: The onset of the disease occurs at birth and the characteristic features include non-recordable electroretinogram (ERG), nystagmus, sluggish or absent pupillary responses and oculo-digital reflexes
evidence.explanation: Nystagmus is described as a characteristic LCA feature in CRB1-associated disease.

steps/6.description: Nystagmus is a characteristic sign of the severe EOSRD/LCA branch, reflecting early and severe visual impairment from birth or infancy.

evidence.snippet: Longitudinal analysis revealed a significant difference between baseline and follow-up best-corrected visual acuity in the 3 subcohorts.
