This IL-11 receptor-signalling arm is an organ-specific instance of the conserved IL-11 signalling module and feeds hepatic stellate cell activation; neutralizing anti-IL-11 (X203) or anti-IL11RA (X209) antibodies block it and reduce liver fibrosis.

evidence.snippet: LF is a wound-healing process characterized by excessive deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins due to the activation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs). In the healthy liver, quiescent HSCs metabolize and store retinoids. Upon fibrogenic activation, quiescent HSCs transdifferentiate into myofibroblasts; lose their vitamin A; upregulate α-smooth muscle actin; and produce proinflammatory soluble mediators, collagens, and inhibitors of ECM degradation. Activated HSCs are the main effector cells during hepatic fibrogenesis.
evidence.explanation: This review definitively establishes HSC activation and transdifferentiation into myofibroblasts as the central mechanism of liver fibrosis and cirrhosis.

evidence.snippet: In addition, the accumulation and activation of profibrogenic macrophages in response to hepatocyte death play a critical role in the initiation of HSC activation and survival.
evidence.explanation: Macrophages play a key role in initiating and maintaining HSC activation, linking hepatocyte injury to stellate cell-mediated fibrosis.

evidence.snippet: Transdifferentiation (or "activation") of hepatic stellate cells is the major cellular source of matrix protein-secreting myofibroblasts, the major driver of liver fibrogenesis.

steps/8.description: Quiescent stellate cells transform into myofibroblasts, producing excessive collagen and extracellular matrix. This is the central event in liver fibrosis.

evidence.snippet: LF is a wound-healing process characterized by excessive deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins due to the activation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs).
evidence.explanation: Establishes excessive ECM deposition as the defining lesion of liver fibrosis, distinct from the stellate-cell activation event that produces it and from the architectural distortion (cirrhosis) it in turn produces.

steps/9.description: Activated hepatic stellate cells/myofibroblasts deposit excessive fibrillar collagen and other extracellular-matrix proteins in the hepatic parenchyma, disrupting sinusoidal exchange and forming the scar tissue that constitutes fibrosis -- the step between stellate-cell activation and the architectural distortion of cirrhosis proper. This is distinct from cirrhosis itself: fibrosis is matrix accumulation, cirrhosis is the architectural end stage downstream of it (see 'Cirrhotic Architectural Distortion').

evidence.snippet: Fibrosis is a pathological scarring process that leads to destruction of organ architecture and impairment of organ function.
evidence.explanation: Supports architectural destruction and organ dysfunction as the consequence of sustained fibrotic scarring. Evidence source is OTHER because this is a mechanistic review synthesizing evidence across fibrotic organs.

steps/10.description: Bridging fibrous septa, regenerative nodules, and vascular remodeling distort the normal hepatic lobular architecture and impair hepatocyte function. This is the architectural end stage proper -- cirrhosis -- and is kept distinct from the upstream matrix-accumulation event ('Excessive Hepatic ECM Deposition'): fibrosis is the lesion, cirrhosis is the structural consequence of enough of it accumulating over enough time.

evidence.snippet: Existing knowledge indicates that the profibrogenic phenotype acquired by sinusoidal cells is the initial factor leading to increased hepatic vascular tone and fibrosis, which cause increased vascular resistance and portal hypertension.

steps/11.description: Fibrosis and architectural distortion, together with a dynamic vasoconstrictive phenotype acquired by sinusoidal cells, raise the resistance the hepatic vasculature offers to portal blood flow. This is the sinusoidal-resistance route the portal hypertension module documents for cirrhosis of any etiology, feeding the disorder-agnostic Portal Hypertension node below.

evidence.snippet: Patients with decompensated liver cirrhosis have significantly impaired synthetic function. Many proteins involved in the coagulation process are synthesized in the liver.

steps/12.description: Reduced hepatocyte mass impairs production of clotting factors, albumin, and other proteins, leading to coagulopathy and hypoalbuminemia.

evidence.snippet: Portal hypertension occurs due to increased resistance of the cirrhotic liver vasculature to portal blood flow and is further aggravated by the hyperdynamic circulatory syndrome.

steps/13.description: Arterial vasodilation in the splanchnic bed increases the volume of blood delivered into the portal system, while systemic vasodilation triggers compensatory cardiac output rise and sodium-retaining neurohormonal activation. This hyperdynamic circulatory syndrome aggravates, rather than compensates, the portal pressure raised by intrahepatic resistance, and is the arm nonselective beta-blockade acts on.

In patient fibroblasts every differentially expressed intronless gene was downregulated, and one of them is ATXN7L3B, which itself couples mRNA export to transcription activation through the TREX-2 and SAGA complexes. That makes the perturbation partly self-reinforcing, and it is the most specific available account of why a general export defect should hit some cells harder than others.

evidence.snippet: Electrophysiological testing and sural nerve biopsy are most compatible with an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, whereas some patients have signs of demyelination.
evidence.explanation: The two investigations that establish the axonal character, and the acknowledged demyelinating minority.

evidence.snippet: The variants were associated with severe childhood onset primarily axonal (four families) or demyelinating (one family) Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: The four-to-one split between axonal and demyelinating presentations in the original families.

steps/5.description: Degeneration of long peripheral motor and sensory axons, confirmed on electrophysiology and sural nerve biopsy as an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy in most patients. A minority have demyelinating features instead, including one of the five original families, so the axonal picture is predominant rather than exclusive.

evidence.snippet: causes distal motor impairment and gait difficulties, often resulting in wheelchair dependency and in difficulties using proximal limbs
evidence.explanation: The motor phenotype and its progression.

steps/6.description: Distal motor impairment with gait difficulty, progressing in many patients to wheelchair dependency and to proximal limb involvement.

evidence.snippet: Electrophysiological testing and sural nerve biopsy are most compatible with an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy
evidence.explanation: The sensorimotor character established by nerve conduction studies and biopsy.

steps/7.description: The sensory half of the sensorimotor neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: Accordingly, fibroblasts of affected individuals from one family demonstrated severe depletion of GANP.
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement of the protein consequence in patient cells.

evidence.snippet: GANP has been described to function as an mRNA export factor
evidence.explanation: The export function whose loss this edge asserts. Graded OTHER because the clause is the paper's background summary of established molecular function rather than a result of the clinical study it introduces.

evidence.snippet: to suppress TDP-43-mediated motor neuron degeneration in flies
evidence.explanation: The fly result that first connected GANP to motor neuron degeneration. Split from the export clause because the two halves of that sentence are different kinds of evidence, and indirect because it is a Drosophila TDP-43 model rather than this disease.

evidence.snippet: Patient fibroblasts showed transcriptome alterations that suggested intron content-dependent regulation of gene expression.
evidence.explanation: The measured transcriptome consequence in patient cells.

evidence.snippet: Thus our results suggest defective mRNA export from nucleus as a potential pathogenic mechanism of axonal degeneration in these patients.
evidence.explanation: The authors present the link between the export defect and axonal degeneration as a suggested potential mechanism, and this entry types the edge accordingly rather than asserting it.

evidence.snippet: This childhood-onset neurologic syndrome is progressive and causes distal motor impairment and gait difficulties, often resulting in wheelchair dependency and in difficulties using proximal limbs.
evidence.explanation: The clinical course produced by the axonal degeneration, including its progression to proximal involvement.

evidence.snippet: severe childhood onset primarily axonal (four families) or demyelinating (one family) Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy
evidence.explanation: Indirect by construction. The quote establishes the Charcot-Marie-Tooth diagnosis, and the sensory arm follows from that diagnosis being sensorimotor by definition rather than from any sensory measurement in the quoted sentence.

evidence.snippet: The identification of MCM3AP variants in affected individuals from multiple centres establishes it as a disease gene for childhood-onset recessively inherited Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy with intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: The statement establishing the gene-disease relationship, and the multi-centre ascertainment behind it.

evidence.snippet: This childhood-onset neurologic syndrome is progressive and causes distal motor impairment and gait difficulties, often resulting in wheelchair dependency
evidence.explanation: The progressive motor impairment that rehabilitation addresses. The cited work characterizes the course and does not evaluate the intervention.

evidence.snippet: Additionally, we elaborate on the importance of rehabilitation intervention.
evidence.explanation: The only statement in the cached literature that recommends rehabilitation for this disease rather than merely describing the impairment it would address. Still not an evaluation of the intervention.

treatments/0.description: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Management is supportive and rehabilitative, directed at the progressive distal weakness and the consequences of loss of ambulation.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Supportive rather than mechanism-directed. Nothing in the cited literature evaluates rehabilitation in this disorder specifically.

evidence.snippet: characteristic claw hands and foot deformities and scoliosis
evidence.explanation: The deformities this management addresses. No disorder-specific outcome evidence exists.

treatments/1.description: Orthotic and surgical management of the foot deformity and scoliosis that accompany the neuropathy, as in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease generally.

evidence.snippet: Our findings expand the genetic spectrum of MCM3AP and suggest that genotype-phenotype correlation would help genetic counseling of MCM3AP in CMT patients.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own statement of the counselling application.

treatments/2.description: Autosomal recessive recurrence counselling. The genotype-phenotype correlation is relevant to prognostic discussion, though the only association reported as established rather than as a trend is delayed independent walking in the null group.

evidence.snippet: Thus our results suggest defective mRNA export from nucleus as a potential pathogenic mechanism of axonal degeneration in these patients.
evidence.explanation: The hedged framing in the disease-defining paper, which is the state of the evidence this gap records.

open_questions/0.rationale: GANP and TREX-2 operate in every nucleus, so selective vulnerability of long peripheral axons is the central unexplained feature of this disease. The best available lead is that the transcriptome changes are structured by intron content rather than being uniform, which could concentrate the effect on a particular set of transcripts. But no work connects that transcript set to axonal length, and the original cohort paper presents the export-to-axonal-degeneration link as a suggestion. This entry types that edge as having unknown intermediates for that reason.

evidence.snippet: The percentage of intellectual disability and loss of ambulation in the null group tended to be greater, although this failed to reach statistical significance.
evidence.explanation: The explicit statement of non-significance that this gap is about.

open_questions/1.rationale:
Two separate lines point the same way: patient fibroblasts show that depleting alleles give more severe phenotypes than Sac3-domain alleles, and cohort analysis finds delayed independent walking in the null group. But the cohort's intellectual disability and loss-of-ambulation comparisons did not reach statistical significance, and the authors say so. With fewer than thirty reported individuals in the largest retrospective series, the question is one of power rather than of contradictory evidence, and this entry quotes the non-significant result rather than rounding it up.
A later retrospective analysis does report a domain-level correlation, at 100% early-onset symptoms, motor delay and cognitive abnormality for alleles outside the Sac3 domain against 26.7% and 46.7% within it, and that result is curated in the genetic section rather than here. It narrows the gap without closing it: it is a different comparison from the null-versus-Sac3 severity question this discussion is about, it is retrospective over the same small published population, and it reports no significance test.

evidence.snippet: MPI is mainly a cytosolic enzyme (but it can be also localised in the plasma membrane) which catalyses the first step of biosynthesis of nucleotide sugar mannose-GDP, that is, interconversion of fructose-6-phosphate to mannose-6-phosphate (Figure 1A).
evidence.explanation: The consensus guideline states the enzymatic reaction catalysed by MPI. Evidence source is OTHER because this is the review's biochemical background synthesis rather than a primary patient observation.

evidence.snippet: In described MPI-CDG patients, enzyme activities were usually very deficient with activities less than 10% of normal values in both leukocytes and fibroblasts.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the residual enzyme activity measured in patients.

evidence.snippet: Phosphomannose isomerase (PMI) deficiency is the cause of a new type of carbohydrate-deficient glycoprotein syndrome (CDGS). The disorder is caused by mutations in the PMI1 gene.
evidence.explanation: The founding report establishing PMI deficiency and MPI mutations as the cause of the disorder.

steps/1.description: Biallelic loss-of-function or hypomorphic variants in MPI reduce the activity of phosphomannose (mannose-6-phosphate) isomerase, the mainly cytosolic enzyme that interconverts fructose-6-phosphate and mannose-6-phosphate. Residual enzyme activity in patient leukocytes and fibroblasts is typically below 10% of normal. Because fructose-6-phosphate is a glycolytic intermediate, the block itself does not cause accumulation of a toxic upstream substrate; the lesion is one of insufficient mannose-6-phosphate supply.

evidence.snippet: Synthesis of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide (LLO), which serves as the sugar donor for the N-glycosylation of secretory proteins, requires conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to mannose-6-phosphate via the phosphomannose isomerase (MPI) enzyme.
evidence.explanation: Places the MPI reaction directly upstream of lipid-linked oligosaccharide synthesis. Evidence source is OTHER because this sentence is the paper's background statement of the pathway rather than a result from its zebrafish experiments.

evidence.snippet: Fluorophore-assisted carbohydrate electrophoresis detected decreased LLO and N-glycans in mpi morphants.
evidence.explanation: A zebrafish MPI-knockdown model with patient-range residual activity directly demonstrates reduced lipid-linked oligosaccharide and N-glycan pools. Model-organism evidence, complementing the human biochemistry.

evidence.snippet: However, the enzymatic block can be therapeutically bypassed by dietary mannose supplementation
evidence.explanation: Establishes that this node is the pharmacologically bypassable step, the basis of D-mannose therapy.

steps/2.description: Mannose-6-phosphate is the committed precursor of GDP-mannose, the mannosyl donor for assembly of the dolichol-linked (lipid-linked) oligosaccharide in the endoplasmic reticulum. In MPI deficiency the endogenous route to mannose-6-phosphate fails and dietary mannose is insufficient to compensate under ordinary conditions, so lipid-linked oligosaccharide synthesis is curtailed and incomplete precursors are transferred to nascent protein - the canonical CDG type I lesion. Plasma mannose is under 10 micromol/L in patients versus 50-100 micromol/L in healthy individuals. This is the step at which exogenous D-mannose therapy re-enters the pathway.

evidence.snippet: Our results in vitro suggest that mannose toxicity in Mpi(-/-) embryos is caused by Man-6-P accumulation, which inhibits glucose metabolism and depletes intracellular ATP.
evidence.explanation: The Mpi-null mouse establishes the mechanism of mannose-6-phosphate toxicity. Model-organism evidence; the human counterpart is the intravenous-mannose case report below.

evidence.snippet: In cell lysates, Man-6-P inhibited hexokinase (70%), phosphoglucose isomerase (65%), and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (85%), but not phosphofructokinase.
evidence.explanation: Biochemical assays identify the specific glycolytic enzymes inhibited by mannose-6-phosphate.

evidence.snippet: We caution that, in patients with MPI-CDG, life-threatening central nervous system disturbances may occur with intravenous mannose treatment.
evidence.explanation: Human clinical confirmation that intravenous mannose can cause severe neurological deterioration in MPI-CDG.

steps/3.description: An iatrogenic mechanism specific to MPI deficiency: because mannose-6-phosphate cannot be isomerised back to fructose-6-phosphate, an excessive mannose load (notably intravenous mannose) allows intracellular mannose-6-phosphate to accumulate. Mannose-6-phosphate inhibits hexokinase, phosphoglucose isomerase and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, suppressing glycolysis and depleting ATP - the "honeybee effect". This underlies reported seizures and stupor during intravenous mannose therapy and the paradoxical worsening of Mpi-null mouse embryos given mannose, and is the reason intravenous mannose is not recommended for stable patients.

evidence.snippet: MPI-CDG can be biochemically characterised by a decreased level of the major tetrasialylated transferrin (Trf) glycoform (tetrasialotransferrin) and an increase of disialotransferrin and asialotransferrin, that is, CDG type I pattern.
evidence.explanation: Documents systemic protein hypoglycosylation via the transferrin readout.

evidence.snippet: The symptoms result from hypoglycosylation of serum- and other glycoproteins.
evidence.explanation: States explicitly that the clinical phenotype is downstream of glycoprotein hypoglycosylation.

steps/4.description: Many secreted and membrane glycoproteins carry absent or truncated N-glycans. The readout is the classic CDG type I serum transferrin pattern - reduced tetrasialotransferrin with increased disialo- and asialotransferrin - which is 100% sensitive but biochemically indistinguishable from PMM2-CDG and other type I disorders. Because glycosylation modifies a large fraction of the secreted proteome, this single lesion degrades many unrelated proteins at once, and the specific organ pattern of MPI-CDG reflects which client glycoproteins are rate-limiting rather than any tissue-restricted expression of MPI.

evidence.snippet: Coagulopathy with typical pattern affecting both procoagulant and anticoagulant factors is reported in almost all patients, with mainly antithrombin (AT) deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the near-universal mixed coagulopathy and its dominant antithrombin component.

evidence.snippet: Congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG), a rare disease, are actually usually associated with antithrombin deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Links the glycosylation defect to antithrombin deficiency as the characteristic coagulation lesion of CDG, the molecular basis for this node.

steps/5.description: Antithrombin, protein C, protein S and factor XI are all N-glycosylated plasma proteins, and their functional levels fall in MPI-CDG. The result is a mixed coagulopathy affecting both procoagulant and anticoagulant arms, so the same patient may thrombose and bleed. Antithrombin deficiency dominates, and the deficits are exacerbated by intercurrent protein-losing enteropathy episodes, dehydration and infection.

evidence.snippet: The diarrhoea is most commonly due to PLE with resulting hypoalbuminaemia.
evidence.explanation: Places protein-losing enteropathy causally upstream of the diarrhoea and hypoalbuminaemia. Evidence source is OTHER because this is the consensus panel's mechanistic interpretation of the pooled case literature.

evidence.snippet: The clinical phenotype is characterized by protein-losing enteropathy, while neurological manifestations prevailing in other types of CDGS are absent.
evidence.explanation: The founding report identifies protein-losing enteropathy as the defining clinical consequence.

steps/6.description: Loss of intestinal wall integrity, attributed to reduced glycoproteins on the enterocyte membrane and/or intestinal lymphangiectasia, produces protein-losing enteropathy with hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, diarrhoea and secondary hypogammaglobulinaemia. Duodenal biopsy may show mild villous atrophy and lymphangiectasia, and both the clinical syndrome and the histology normalise on mannose.

evidence.snippet: However, the most characteristic lesion mimics those seen in congenital hepatic fibrosis, with an excess of dilated bile duct structures in ductal plate configuration in the portal tracts
evidence.explanation: Identifies the characteristic hepatic histopathology.

evidence.snippet: As the typical histological lesions represent congenital/developmental abnormalities of the liver (ie, ductal plate malformation), they do not respond to mannose therapy.
evidence.explanation: States the mechanistic reason the hepatic arm is refractory to mannose.

evidence.snippet: Liver fibrosis persisted despite treatment, but two patients showed improved liver architecture during follow-up.
evidence.explanation: Long-term treated follow-up confirms persistence of fibrosis on therapy.

steps/7.description: Essentially all patients have some degree of liver involvement. The characteristic lesion is a developmental one - an excess of dilated bile duct structures in a ductal plate configuration, mimicking congenital hepatic fibrosis, together with hepatomegaly, fibrosis and sometimes steatosis. Because it is a congenital/developmental abnormality rather than an ongoing glycosylation-dependent process, it does not reverse with mannose and can progress to portal hypertension, oesophageal varices and hepatopulmonary syndrome. This mannose-refractory arm is the principal determinant of long-term morbidity.

evidence.snippet: Thrombotic events often complicate acute infections and dehydration episodes. These are mainly deep vein thromboses of the lower extremities.
evidence.explanation: Describes the triggers and typical site of thrombosis in the pooled cohort.

evidence.snippet: In summary, we present the first MPI-CDG patient with severe cerebral venous sinus thrombosis as first and only symptom of disease manifestation.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that the thrombotic arm alone can constitute the entire clinical presentation.

steps/8.description: Thrombosis typically complicates intercurrent infection or dehydration and is most often deep venous thrombosis of the lower limbs, but cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, pulmonary embolism and intracardiac thrombus are reported and may be the presenting event. Bleeding is less frequent but can be life-threatening, chiefly diffuse intestinal bleeding or variceal haemorrhage.

evidence.snippet: The most common cause of hypoglycaemia in these patients was hyperinsulinism (HH), which is present in more than two-third of hypoglycaemic patients.
evidence.explanation: Establishes hyperinsulinism as the predominant hypoglycaemia mechanism.

evidence.snippet: However, the exact cause of HH in CDG patients is still unknown.
evidence.explanation: Explicitly flags the mechanism of hyperinsulinism as unresolved, so this node's proposed beta-cell mechanism is only partially supported.

steps/9.description: Hypoglycaemia affects most patients and is most often hyperinsulinaemic. The mechanism is unresolved; hypoglycosylation of beta-cell membrane proteins such as the sulfonylurea receptor SUR1 has been proposed, supported by altered insulin secretion in hypoglycosylated murine beta cells. A minority of patients are hypoglycaemic without hyperinsulinism. Hypoglycaemia responds to mannose in both groups.

evidence.snippet: In contrast with PMM2-CDG, facial dysmorphia, atypical fat pads, inverted nipples, and skeletal deformities are not present in MPI-CDG patients.
evidence.explanation: Documents the absence of the classic CDG dysmorphic pattern in MPI-CDG.

evidence.snippet: no cerebellar hypoplasia was noted, as it is typical in other CDG.
evidence.explanation: Neuroimaging in reported patients shows the absence of the cerebellar hypoplasia characteristic of other CDG subtypes.

evidence.snippet: The exogenous mannose pathway is also a possible explanation for the absence of developmental impairment in MPI-CDG as circulating maternal mannose reduces the prenatal glycosylation defect in cerebral tissues.
evidence.explanation: The maternal-mannose rescue account of neurologic sparing is presented by the consensus panel as a hypothesis rather than an established mechanism, so this quote bears on the node only indirectly.

steps/10.description: The convergent multisystem outflow of hypoglycosylation in MPI-CDG is hepatic, gastrointestinal, endocrine, coagulation and immune, but - unlike almost every other CDG - not neurologic. Cognitive development and brain imaging are typically normal, cerebellar hypoplasia is absent, and the dysmorphic, fat-pad, inverted-nipple and skeletal features of PMM2-CDG do not occur. A proposed explanation is that circulating maternal and dietary mannose partially rescues glycosylation in developing cerebral tissue, consistent with the zebrafish finding that mannose rescue is effective only within an early developmental window.

evidence.snippet: The clinical phenotype is characterized by protein-losing enteropathy, while neurological manifestations prevailing in other types of CDGS are absent.
evidence.explanation: The founding report defines protein-losing enteropathy as the characteristic phenotype.

evidence.snippet: chronic diarrhea (41/46), vomiting (23/27), hepatomegaly (39/44), hepatic fibrosis (20/37), protein-losing enteropathy (30/36), elevated serum transaminases (24/34), hyperinsulinemic-hypoglycemia (24/34), hypoalbuminemia (33/38), prolonged coagulation (26/30), splenomegaly (13/21), non-pitting edema (14/20), failure to thrive (13/36), portal hypertension (4/9), epilepsy (2/17), thrombosis (12/14), and abnormally elevated leukocytes (5)
evidence.explanation: Protein-losing enteropathy in 30/36 assessed patients (83%) supports the VERY_FREQUENT band (80-100%).

steps/11.description: Enteric protein loss with hypoalbuminaemia is the cardinal and often presenting manifestation of MPI-CDG, and was the feature that defined the disorder. Faecal alpha-1-antitrypsin is elevated 3- to 20-fold when measured.

evidence.snippet: The diarrhoea is most commonly due to PLE with resulting hypoalbuminaemia.
evidence.explanation: Directly links protein-losing enteropathy to hypoalbuminaemia. Evidence source is OTHER because this is the consensus panel's mechanistic interpretation of the pooled case literature, matching how this sentence is graded elsewhere in the entry.

evidence.snippet: hypoalbuminemia (33/38), prolonged coagulation (26/30), splenomegaly (13/21), non-pitting edema (14/20), failure to thrive (13/36)
evidence.explanation: Hypoalbuminaemia in 33/38 assessed patients (87%) supports the VERY_FREQUENT band.

steps/12.description: Hypoalbuminaemia is the biochemical consequence of enteric protein loss and can be severe enough to require repeated intravenous albumin infusions.

evidence.snippet: hypoalbuminemia (33/38), prolonged coagulation (26/30), splenomegaly (13/21), non-pitting edema (14/20), failure to thrive (13/36)
evidence.explanation: Non-pitting oedema in 14/20 assessed patients (70%) supports the FREQUENT band (30-79%).

evidence.snippet: Individuals who are deficient in MPI present with bleeding, diarrhea, edema, gastrointestinal bleeding and liver fibrosis.
evidence.explanation: This modelling paper's clinical summary of the human disorder lists oedema among the presenting features; the quoted statement is about human patients, not the zebrafish model. Evidence source is OTHER because the sentence is the paper's background synthesis of prior human reports rather than primary data of its own.

steps/13.description: Oedema, characteristically non-pitting and up to anasarca in the earliest described cluster of patients, results from the hypoalbuminaemia of protein-losing enteropathy.

evidence.snippet: Diarrhoea is the most common gastrointestinal symptom.
evidence.explanation: Establishes diarrhoea as the leading gastrointestinal feature.

evidence.snippet: chronic diarrhea (41/46), vomiting (23/27), hepatomegaly (39/44), hepatic fibrosis (20/37), protein-losing enteropathy (30/36)
evidence.explanation: Chronic diarrhoea in 41/46 assessed patients (89%) supports the VERY_FREQUENT band.

steps/14.description: Diarrhoea is the single most common gastrointestinal symptom and may be isolated or, more often, combined with vomiting; episodes leading to dehydration frequently require hospital admission.

evidence.snippet: The presenting symptoms were mainly combination of gastrointestinal involvement (cyclic vomiting, PLE and failure to thrive, n = 26), hypoglycaemia (n = 15), hepatic involvement (elevation of transaminases, hepatomegaly, liver fibrosis, n = 14), and coagulation complications (laboratory coagulopathy, thrombosis, intestinal bleeding, n = 7).
evidence.explanation: Cyclic vomiting is named among the presenting gastrointestinal features.

evidence.snippet: chronic diarrhea (41/46), vomiting (23/27), hepatomegaly (39/44)
evidence.explanation: Vomiting in 23/27 assessed patients (85%) supports the VERY_FREQUENT band.

steps/15.description: Recurrent, sometimes cyclic vomiting is a characteristic presenting symptom and typically accompanies the diarrhoea.

evidence.snippet: Duodenal biopsies, when performed, reveal a mild villous atrophy
evidence.explanation: Documents the duodenal histology reported in MPI-CDG.

steps/16.description: Duodenal biopsy, when performed, may show mild villous atrophy, which normalises histologically after mannose treatment. Biopsy can nevertheless be normal even in patients with documented protein-losing enteropathy, so frequency is not stated.

evidence.snippet: Duodenal biopsies, when performed, reveal a mild villous atrophy2,8,29,42,43,48,50 and less frequently lymphangiectasia.
evidence.explanation: Reports lymphangiectasia on duodenal biopsy in a subset of patients (the embedded digits are the guideline's inline reference numbers).

steps/17.description: Intestinal lymphangiectasia is reported less frequently than villous atrophy and is one of the two proposed mechanisms of enteric protein loss.

evidence.snippet: The gastrointestinal impairment often leads to malnutrition/failure to thrive, which were reported in two-thirds of patients, although the anthropometric measurements were available in only half of them.
evidence.explanation: "Two-thirds of patients" maps to the FREQUENT band (30-79%).

evidence.snippet: non-pitting edema (14/20), failure to thrive (13/36), portal hypertension (4/9)
evidence.explanation: Failure to thrive in 13/36 assessed patients (36%) in the larger review also falls in the FREQUENT band, at its lower end.

steps/18.description: Malnutrition and failure to thrive follow the recurrent vomiting and diarrhoea; severe cases require nasogastric, gastrostomy or parenteral feeding.

evidence.snippet: Growth restriction was documented in four patients.
evidence.explanation: Four of the 35 reviewed patients (approximately 11%) maps to the OCCASIONAL band (5-29%).

steps/19.description: Growth restriction independent of failure to thrive is documented in a minority of patients and has been attributed to hypoglycosylation of IGFBP-3 and the acid-labile subunit, with catch-up growth on mannose.

evidence.snippet: Hepatomegaly is the most common clinical sign, sometimes associated with splenomegaly that is not initially present in the case of early diagnosis, but that appears in the first year of life.
evidence.explanation: Names hepatomegaly as the most common hepatic sign.

evidence.snippet: chronic diarrhea (41/46), vomiting (23/27), hepatomegaly (39/44), hepatic fibrosis (20/37)
evidence.explanation: Hepatomegaly in 39/44 assessed patients (89%) supports the VERY_FREQUENT band.

steps/20.description: Hepatomegaly is the most common clinical hepatic sign, sometimes accompanied by splenomegaly appearing during the first year of life.

evidence.snippet: Liver involvement in MPI-CDG is one of the most common features. Patients often present with mild hepatopathy, hepatomegaly, and hepatic fibrosis.
evidence.explanation: Names hepatic fibrosis among the common hepatic features.

evidence.snippet: hepatomegaly (39/44), hepatic fibrosis (20/37), protein-losing enteropathy (30/36)
evidence.explanation: Hepatic fibrosis in 20/37 assessed patients (54%) supports the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: Liver fibrosis persisted despite treatment, but two patients showed improved liver architecture during follow-up.
evidence.explanation: Confirms persistence and progression of fibrosis under treatment.

steps/21.description: Liver fibrosis is a defining and progressive feature. Unlike the digestive, hypoglycaemic and coagulation manifestations, it does not respond to mannose and may advance to cirrhosis with its attendant complications.

evidence.snippet: However, the most characteristic lesion mimics those seen in congenital hepatic fibrosis, with an excess of dilated bile duct structures in ductal plate configuration in the portal tracts
evidence.explanation: Directly describes the ductal plate malformation on liver biopsy.

steps/22.description: The most characteristic hepatic lesion is an excess of dilated bile duct structures in ductal plate configuration in the portal tracts, mimicking congenital hepatic fibrosis; von Meyenburg complexes have also been described.

evidence.snippet: protein-losing enteropathy (30/36), elevated serum transaminases (24/34), hyperinsulinemic-hypoglycemia (24/34)
evidence.explanation: Elevated transaminases in 24/34 assessed patients (71%) supports the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) and bilirubin levels are often normal.
evidence.explanation: Documents the sparing of GGT and bilirubin that defines the characteristic liver-enzyme pattern.

steps/23.description: Transaminases are commonly, usually mildly, elevated, but can rise 30- to 40-fold during acute decompensation and may also be normal despite established liver involvement. GGT and bilirubin are often normal, giving a characteristic pattern.

evidence.snippet: The rare but serious complications are portal hypertension with or without oesophageal varices and hepatopulmonary syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Identifies portal hypertension as an uncommon but serious hepatic complication.

evidence.snippet: On treatment, two patients developed severe portal hypertension, two developed venous thrombosis, and 1 displayed altered kidney function.
evidence.explanation: Two of nine treated patients developed severe portal hypertension during long-term follow-up.

steps/24.description: Portal hypertension is the main hepatic complication in adulthood and may be accompanied by oesophageal varices or, rarely, hepatopulmonary syndrome. It develops despite mannose therapy and warrants lifelong surveillance. A frequency band is deliberately omitted: the consensus guideline calls it a "rare but serious" complication, whereas the 2023 review reports 4/9 among the few patients in whom it was specifically assessed, an ascertainment-biased denominator.

evidence.snippet: The main complication in adulthood is the portal hypertension with oesophageal varices.
evidence.explanation: Names oesophageal varices as the adult hepatic complication.

steps/25.description: Oesophageal varices arise from portal hypertension and, with diffuse intestinal bleeding, constitute the principal fatal haemorrhagic risk.

evidence.snippet: prolonged coagulation (26/30), splenomegaly (13/21), non-pitting edema (14/20)
evidence.explanation: Splenomegaly in 13/21 assessed patients (62%) supports the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: Hepatomegaly is the most common clinical sign, sometimes associated with splenomegaly that is not initially present in the case of early diagnosis, but that appears in the first year of life.
evidence.explanation: Documents splenomegaly appearing during the first year of life.

steps/26.description: Splenomegaly accompanies hepatomegaly in many patients and, with thrombocytopenia, is a clinical marker of developing portal hypertension.

evidence.snippet: Liver biopsy, when performed, can often show liver fibrosis1,2,28,29,35,36,39–48 or steatosis.
evidence.explanation: The guideline lists steatosis among the liver-biopsy findings, supported by a small minority of the reviewed case reports (its three inline citations), consistent with the OCCASIONAL band. The embedded digits are the guideline's inline reference numbers.

steps/27.description: Steatosis is reported on liver biopsy in a subset of patients alongside fibrosis.

evidence.snippet: Hypoglycaemia has been observed in the majority of reported MPI-CDG patients.
evidence.explanation: "Majority" maps to the FREQUENT band (30-79%).

evidence.snippet: Hypoglycaemia is frequently associated with MPI-CDG and, it can be a presenting and rarely even the only sign.
evidence.explanation: Confirms hypoglycaemia can be the sole presenting manifestation.

steps/28.description: Hypoglycaemia is observed in the majority of patients, usually first in infancy, and can be the presenting or even the only sign. It may be asymptomatic or cause seizures, unresponsiveness and apnoea.

evidence.snippet: The most common cause of hypoglycaemia in these patients was hyperinsulinism (HH), which is present in more than two-third of hypoglycaemic patients.
evidence.explanation: Hyperinsulinism in more than two-thirds of the hypoglycaemic patients.

evidence.snippet: elevated serum transaminases (24/34), hyperinsulinemic-hypoglycemia (24/34), hypoalbuminemia (33/38)
evidence.explanation: Hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia in 24/34 assessed patients (71%) supports the FREQUENT band.

steps/29.description: Hyperinsulinism accounts for more than two-thirds of hypoglycaemia in MPI-CDG. It responds to mannose and, when needed, to diazoxide.

evidence.snippet: Coagulopathy with typical pattern affecting both procoagulant and anticoagulant factors is reported in almost all patients, with mainly antithrombin (AT) deficiency.
evidence.explanation: "Almost all patients" maps to the VERY_FREQUENT band (80-100%), with antithrombin named as the principal deficiency.

evidence.snippet: hypoalbuminemia (33/38), prolonged coagulation (26/30), splenomegaly (13/21)
evidence.explanation: Prolonged coagulation in 26/30 assessed patients (87%) corroborates the VERY_FREQUENT band for the coagulopathy of which antithrombin deficiency is the dominant component.

evidence.snippet: CDG screening should be included into the routine diagnostic work‐up in all patients presenting with unexplained coagulation disorder, especially when comprising AT deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Reinforces antithrombin deficiency as the characteristic and diagnostically actionable coagulation abnormality.

steps/30.description: Antithrombin deficiency is the dominant coagulation abnormality of MPI-CDG and reflects hypoglycosylation of this heavily N-glycosylated inhibitor. It can be the diagnostic clue in an otherwise unexplained thrombophilia.

evidence.snippet: Deficit in protein C (PC) and in factor XI (FXI) is also frequently observed, and protein S (PS) can also be decreased.
evidence.explanation: "Frequently observed" maps to the FREQUENT band.

steps/31.description: Protein C deficiency is frequently observed alongside antithrombin deficiency; protein S can also be reduced.

evidence.snippet: Deficit in protein C (PC) and in factor XI (FXI) is also frequently observed, and protein S (PS) can also be decreased.
evidence.explanation: "Frequently observed" maps to the FREQUENT band.

steps/32.description: Factor XI deficiency is part of the characteristic mixed MPI-CDG coagulopathy and is a specific perioperative consideration, since factor XI concentrate and recombinant factor VIIa are not recommended because of thrombotic risk.

evidence.snippet: Thrombotic events often complicate acute infections and dehydration episodes. These are mainly deep vein thromboses of the lower extremities.
evidence.explanation: Identifies deep venous thrombosis as the typical thrombotic event.

evidence.snippet: portal hypertension (4/9), epilepsy (2/17), thrombosis (12/14)
evidence.explanation: Records thrombosis in 12/14 assessed patients, the higher of the two conflicting denominators noted in the description.

steps/33.description: Thrombosis, most often deep venous thrombosis of the lower limbs, typically complicates intercurrent infection or dehydration and may be multiple and recurrent. No thrombotic events have been reported in patients maintained on mannose. A frequency band is omitted because the available denominators conflict: overt coagulation complications were the presenting feature in only 7 of 35 patients in the consensus review, whereas thrombosis was recorded in 12 of the 14 patients in whom the 2023 review could assess it.

evidence.snippet: In summary, we present the first MPI-CDG patient with severe cerebral venous sinus thrombosis as first and only symptom of disease manifestation.
evidence.explanation: Case report documenting cerebral venous sinus thrombosis as the presenting event.

steps/34.description: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is a reported thrombotic site and has been described as the first and only presenting symptom of MPI-CDG, requiring thrombectomy and decompressive surgery.

evidence.snippet: Bleeding is less frequent but it can be life threatening.
evidence.explanation: Establishes bleeding as the less frequent but life-threatening arm of the coagulopathy.

evidence.snippet: Bleeding episodes mainly affects gastrointestinal tract and may be associated with oesophageal varices or digestive ulcers.
evidence.explanation: Localises the bleeding to the gastrointestinal tract and names the variceal and ulcer associations.

evidence.snippet: The same patient can both suffer from thrombosis and bleeding.
evidence.explanation: Documents that thrombosis and bleeding co-occur in the same patient, the hallmark of the mixed coagulopathy.

steps/35.description: Bleeding is the less frequent arm of the mixed coagulopathy but can be life-threatening. It chiefly affects the gastrointestinal tract - ranging from easy bruising through repeated diffuse intestinal bleeding to fatal variceal haemorrhage with hematemesis - and may be associated with oesophageal varices or digestive ulcers; the same patient can suffer both thrombosis and bleeding. A frequency band is omitted because the guideline reports clinical bleeding without a denominator.

evidence.snippet: Immunoglobulin deficiency due to PLE (characteristic by decreased levels of IgG but normal levels of IgA and IgM) was described in six patients.
evidence.explanation: Six of 35 patients (approximately 17%) maps to the OCCASIONAL band.

steps/36.description: Immunoglobulin deficiency secondary to protein-losing enteropathy, with reduced IgG but preserved IgA and IgM, is documented in a minority of patients.

evidence.snippet: This pattern is 100% sensitive but non-specific (eg, indistinguishable from PMM2-CDG) and it has been reported in all MPI-CDG patients except those diagnosed post-mortem on basis of symptoms and/or MPI gene analysis in parents or siblings.
evidence.explanation: Reported in all living ascertained patients, supporting VERY_FREQUENT.

steps/37.description: Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing shows a CDG type I pattern in all clinically ascertained patients. The pattern is 100% sensitive but is indistinguishable from PMM2-CDG and other type I disorders, so MPI enzyme assay and/or MPI sequencing is required for the diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: Seizures were documented in six patients, but they were secondary in all cases and no chronical antiepileptic treatment was necessary.
evidence.explanation: Six of 35 patients (approximately 17%) maps to the OCCASIONAL band, and the statement establishes that seizures are always secondary.

evidence.snippet: portal hypertension (4/9), epilepsy (2/17), thrombosis (12/14)
evidence.explanation: Epilepsy in 2/17 assessed patients (12%) independently supports the OCCASIONAL band.

steps/38.description: Seizures occur in a minority of patients and are always secondary - to hypoglycaemia, to cerebral thrombosis, or as an adverse effect of intravenous mannose. Chronic antiepileptic treatment is not required.

edges/1.description: Reduced mannose-6-phosphate supply limits the downstream nucleotide-sugar pool required to build the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide precursor.

edges/2.description: Incomplete lipid-linked oligosaccharide precursors are transferred to nascent glycoproteins, producing systemic hypoglycosylation.

edges/3.description: Hypoglycosylation of enterocyte surface glycoproteins is the proposed mechanism of intestinal barrier failure and enteric protein loss.

edges/4.description: Antithrombin, protein C, protein S and factor XI are N-glycoproteins whose plasma levels fall when glycosylation is impaired.

edges/5.description: Hypoglycosylation is proposed to alter beta-cell insulin secretion, although the precise mechanism remains unresolved.

edges/6.description: Prenatal and early hypoglycosylation is associated with a developmental biliary lesion and progressive fibrosis that, unlike the other arms, does not reverse with mannose.

edges/7.description: The convergent multisystem outflow of proteome-wide hypoglycosylation, distinguished in MPI-CDG by the near-absence of neurologic involvement.

evidence.snippet: MPI-CDG can be biochemically characterised by a decreased level of the major tetrasialylated transferrin (Trf) glycoform (tetrasialotransferrin) and an increase of disialotransferrin and asialotransferrin, that is, CDG type I pattern.
evidence.explanation: The transferrin pattern is stated to be the biochemical characterisation of the glycosylation defect itself.

edges/8.description: Hypoglycosylated serum transferrin - reduced tetrasialotransferrin with increased disialo- and asialotransferrin - is the direct serum readout of this node and the diagnostic screening phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Other endocrine symptoms seen in MPI-CDG are growth restriction due to ALS and IGFBP-3 hypoglycosylation, hypothyroidism and benign TBG deficiency, but those are much less common.
evidence.explanation: The consensus panel attributes the growth restriction to ALS and IGFBP-3 hypoglycosylation. Evidence source is OTHER because this is the panel's mechanistic synthesis, resting on single documented cases.

edges/9.description: Growth restriction in a minority of patients is attributed to hypoglycosylation of the IGF-axis carrier proteins IGFBP-3 and the acid-labile subunit, with catch-up growth once mannose restores glycosylation.

edges/10.description: The intestinal barrier failure of this node manifests clinically as enteric protein loss - the cardinal phenotype that defined the disorder.

evidence.snippet: The diarrhoea is most commonly due to PLE with resulting hypoalbuminaemia.
evidence.explanation: The consensus panel places PLE causally upstream of the diarrhoea. Evidence source is OTHER because this is the panel's mechanistic interpretation of the pooled case literature.

edges/11.description: The chronic diarrhoea of MPI-CDG is attributed by the consensus panel to the protein-losing enteropathy of this node.

evidence.snippet: The diarrhoea is most commonly due to PLE with resulting hypoalbuminaemia.
evidence.explanation: Names hypoalbuminaemia as the direct result of the protein-losing enteropathy. Evidence source is OTHER because this is the panel's mechanistic interpretation of the pooled case literature.

edges/12.description: Enteric loss of albumin, not hepatic synthetic failure, is the stated cause of the hypoalbuminaemia in the majority of patients.

evidence.snippet: The severity of hypoalbuminaemia can vary, it can often leads to oedema
evidence.explanation: The pooled case literature links the hypoalbuminaemia directly to the oedema.

edges/13.description: Oedema follows the hypoalbuminaemia of enteric protein loss through reduced plasma oncotic pressure.

evidence.snippet: One week after the start of mannose treatment, the vomiting and diarrhea symptoms disappeared completely and did not show any side effects.
evidence.explanation: Remission of vomiting on mannose ties it to the glycosylation-dependent gastrointestinal arm; the evidence is indirect for the mechanistic routing because the intermediate steps are not established.

edges/14.description: Recurrent, often cyclic vomiting is part of the gastrointestinal arm of the disease and remits with the other digestive symptoms on mannose, tying it to the glycosylation-dependent intestinal lesion, although its specific mechanism has not been dissected.

evidence.snippet: The gastrointestinal impairment often leads to malnutrition/failure to thrive, which were reported in two-thirds of patients, although the anthropometric measurements were available in only half of them.
evidence.explanation: States that the gastrointestinal impairment leads to the malnutrition and failure to thrive.

edges/15.description: Chronic enteric protein loss with recurrent diarrhoea and vomiting produces malnutrition and failure to thrive.

evidence.snippet: Duodenal biopsies, when performed, reveal a mild villous atrophy
evidence.explanation: Documents the biopsy lesion belonging to the intestinal arm of the disease.

edges/16.description: Mild villous atrophy is a histological correlate of the enterocyte lesion on duodenal biopsy and normalises on mannose.

evidence.snippet: Duodenal biopsies, when performed, reveal a mild villous atrophy2,8,29,42,43,48,50 and less frequently lymphangiectasia.
evidence.explanation: Documents lymphangiectasia as a biopsy lesion of the intestinal arm (the embedded digits are the guideline's inline reference numbers).

edges/17.description: Lymphangiectasia is the second duodenal biopsy lesion of the intestinal arm and one of the two proposed routes of enteric protein loss.

evidence.snippet: Immunoglobulin deficiency due to PLE (characteristic by decreased levels of IgG but normal levels of IgA and IgM) was described in six patients.
evidence.explanation: States the immunoglobulin deficiency is due to the protein-losing enteropathy.

edges/18.description: Enteric loss of immunoglobulin G produces the secondary hypogammaglobulinaemia, with IgA and IgM preserved.

edges/19.description: The imbalance of procoagulant and anticoagulant glycoproteins destabilises haemostasis in both directions.

edges/20.description: Antithrombin, a heavily N-glycosylated inhibitor, is the dominant deficiency produced by this node and the characteristic laboratory clue.

evidence.snippet: Deficit in protein C (PC) and in factor XI (FXI) is also frequently observed, and protein S (PS) can also be decreased.
evidence.explanation: Documents the protein C deficit within the characteristic coagulation pattern of the glycosylation defect.

edges/21.description: Protein C is among the anticoagulant glycoproteins whose functional levels fall with impaired glycosylation.

evidence.snippet: Deficit in protein C (PC) and in factor XI (FXI) is also frequently observed, and protein S (PS) can also be decreased.
evidence.explanation: Documents the factor XI deficit within the characteristic coagulation pattern of the glycosylation defect.

edges/22.description: Factor XI is the principal procoagulant glycoprotein reduced in MPI-CDG, completing the mixed coagulopathy.

evidence.snippet: Thrombotic events often complicate acute infections and dehydration episodes. These are mainly deep vein thromboses of the lower extremities.
evidence.explanation: Identifies deep venous thrombosis as the main thrombotic event of the destabilised haemostasis.

edges/23.description: Deep venous thrombosis of the lower limbs is the most common realisation of the thrombotic tendency, typically during infection or dehydration.

edges/24.description: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is a reported site of the thrombotic tendency and can be the presenting event of the disease.

evidence.snippet: In two patients, the seizures were secondary to cerebral thrombosis
evidence.explanation: Attributes seizures in two patients directly to cerebral thrombosis.

edges/25.description: Seizures in MPI-CDG can be secondary to cerebral thrombosis with infarction, one of the three documented secondary seizure mechanisms.

evidence.snippet: Bleeding is less frequent but it can be life threatening.
evidence.explanation: Documents the bleeding arm of the haemostatic imbalance in the pooled cohort.

edges/26.description: The haemorrhagic arm of the destabilised haemostasis manifests chiefly as gastrointestinal bleeding, from diffuse intestinal bleeding to life-threatening haemorrhage.

edges/27.description: The dysregulated insulin secretion of this node manifests clinically as hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia.

evidence.snippet: Hypoglycaemia results mainly from HH, although the insulin level can as well be normal.
evidence.explanation: States that hyperinsulinism is the main cause of the hypoglycaemia while acknowledging the non-hyperinsulinaemic minority.

edges/28.description: Hyperinsulinism is the predominant cause of the hypoglycaemia of MPI-CDG; a minority of patients are hypoglycaemic with normal insulin, so this edge accounts for most but not all episodes.

evidence.snippet: Six patients presented symptomatic hypoglycaemia with seizures
evidence.explanation: Documents seizures as a manifestation of symptomatic hypoglycaemia in the pooled cohort.

edges/29.description: Hypoglycaemic seizures in early infancy are one of the three documented secondary seizure mechanisms in MPI-CDG.

edges/30.description: The ductal plate malformation is the defining developmental lesion of this node, seen as an excess of dilated bile duct structures on biopsy.

edges/31.description: Progressive, mannose-refractory fibrosis is the core tissue outcome of this node and the principal determinant of long-term morbidity.

edges/32.description: Hepatomegaly is the most common clinical sign of the hepatic involvement encompassed by this node.

edges/33.description: The hepatopathy of this node produces the usually mild transaminase elevation, with characteristic sparing of GGT and bilirubin.

edges/34.description: Steatosis is one of the biopsy findings within the hepatic lesion of this node, reported alongside fibrosis in a minority of patients.

evidence.snippet: The main complication in adulthood is the portal hypertension with oesophageal varices.
evidence.explanation: Identifies portal hypertension as the adult complication of the hepatic lesion.

edges/35.description: The progressive fibrotic-biliary lesion advances to portal hypertension, the main hepatic complication of adulthood, despite mannose therapy.

evidence.snippet: The main complication in adulthood is the portal hypertension with oesophageal varices.
evidence.explanation: Ties the varices to the portal hypertension of the hepatic lesion.

edges/36.description: Oesophageal varices arise from the portal hypertension produced by the progressive hepatic lesion.

evidence.snippet: For patients with portal hypertension (ie, thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly or collateral circulation on abdominal ultrasound)
evidence.explanation: The guideline's surveillance criteria treat splenomegaly as a clinical indicator of portal hypertension, supporting the routing of this edge through portal venous congestion. Directness is INDIRECT because the quote is diagnostic-criteria phrasing rather than an explicit causal statement, and evidence source is OTHER because it is a panel recommendation.

edges/37.description: Splenomegaly accompanies the hepatic involvement, appearing during the first year of life, and is treated by the guideline as one of the clinical indicators of developing portal hypertension.

evidence.snippet: Bleeding from oesophageal varices and hematemesis is less common.
evidence.explanation: Documents variceal bleeding and hematemesis as the hepatic route to gastrointestinal haemorrhage.

edges/38.description: Variceal rupture from the portal hypertension of the progressive hepatic lesion is the second route to gastrointestinal bleeding, distinct from the coagulopathy-driven route.

evidence.snippet: Generalised convulsions with acute deterioration of mental status were described as a possible adverse effect of mannose therapy with complete restitution after glucose bolus.
evidence.explanation: Documents convulsions as an adverse effect of mannose therapy, the clinical counterpart of this node's toxicity mechanism.

edges/39.description: Iatrogenic seizures during intravenous mannose therapy are attributed to mannose-6-phosphate accumulation with glycolytic inhibition and ATP depletion - one of the three documented secondary seizure mechanisms.

evidence.snippet: CDG-Ib is caused by a deficiency of mannose-6-phosphate isomerase (synonym: phosphomannose isomerase, EC 5.3.1.8), due to mutations in the MPI gene.
evidence.explanation: Establishes MPI as the disease gene.

evidence.snippet: The gene is composed of 8 exons and spans only 5 kb.
evidence.explanation: Defines the genomic structure that underpins routine sequencing.

evidence.snippet: The most common variants are c.656G > A (p. Arg219Gln), c.457G > A (p.Arg152Gln), and c.884G > A (p.Arg295His), which all together form about one half of all alleles.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the recurrent variants and their allelic burden.

evidence.snippet: Among 28 published patients with known genotype, 20 different pathogenic variants were described (summarised in Table 3) with 17 missense variants, 2 frameshift-causing variants, and 1 splicing defect.
evidence.explanation: Characterises the variant spectrum as predominantly missense.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis was confirmed by sequence analysis of the MPI gene revealing a homozygous missense mutation (c.656G>A) causing replacement of arginine by glutamine (p.R219Q). However, the woman had never experienced any clinical manifestations associated with MPI-CDG.
evidence.explanation: Documents clinically asymptomatic homozygosity for the commonest variant, the basis of the incomplete-penetrance claim.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic pathogenic variants in MPI (15q24.1), an eight-exon gene spanning only 5 kb, cause MPI-CDG. Missense variants predominate, consistent with survival requiring residual activity. Three recurrent variants - c.656G>A (p.Arg219Gln), c.457G>A (p.Arg152Gln) and c.884G>A (p.Arg295His) - together account for roughly half of reported alleles. p.Arg219Gln, the first variant identified, has been found homozygous in clinically asymptomatic adults, indicating incomplete penetrance or the action of unknown modifiers; neither residual enzyme activity nor carbohydrate-deficient transferrin reliably predicts clinical severity.

evidence.snippet: Daily oral mannose administration is a successful therapy for this new type of CDG syndrome classified as CDGS type Ib.
evidence.explanation: The founding report establishing oral mannose as effective therapy.

evidence.snippet: Oral mannose is recommended treatment for digestive symptoms, coagulopathy and hypoglycaemia, although it does not treat the liver symptoms in MPI-CDG.
evidence.explanation: Consensus recommendation delimiting exactly which disease arms respond.

evidence.snippet: The recommended mannose dose ranges from 150 to 170 mg/kg/dose four to five times daily.
evidence.explanation: Consensus dosing recommendation.

evidence.snippet: The majority of patients (26/30) showed clinical symptoms, and laboratory results improved after oral mannose administration.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the treated-response rate across the published literature.

evidence.snippet: One week after the start of mannose treatment, the vomiting and diarrhea symptoms disappeared completely and did not show any side effects.
evidence.explanation: Documents the characteristic rapid clinical response in an index case.

evidence.snippet: The main side effects of mannose were abdominal pain and diarrhoea, which were documented in 40% of patients and improved either spontaneously or with a dose adjustment.
evidence.explanation: Documents the adverse-effect profile that qualifies the treatment recommendation.

evidence.snippet: Poor compliance with D-mannose was correlated with recurrence of diarrhea, thrombosis, and abnormal biological parameters including coagulation factors and transferrin profiles.
evidence.explanation: Fifteen-year follow-up establishing the need for lifelong, compliant therapy.

treatments/0.description: Oral D-mannose is the disease-specific therapy and the reason MPI-CDG is one of the few treatable CDGs. Exogenous mannose is phosphorylated by hexokinase to mannose-6-phosphate, entering the N-glycosylation pathway downstream of the MPI block. The recommended dose is 150-170 mg/kg per dose, four to five times daily, started as soon as the diagnosis is made and continued lifelong. It corrects the digestive symptoms, hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy, but it does not treat the hepatic disease. Clinical response usually begins within a week while biochemical abnormalities take months to stabilise. Abdominal pain and diarrhoea are the main side effects. Poor compliance is associated with relapse.

evidence.snippet: Dietary supplementation of mannose can reverse clinical symptoms by entering the N-glycosylation pathway downstream of MPI.
evidence.explanation: States the bypass mechanism explicitly.

evidence.snippet: MPI-CDG patients can be treated with oral mannose supplements, which is converted to mannose-6-phosphate through a minor complementary metabolic pathway, restoring protein glycosylation and ameliorating most symptoms, although liver disease continues to progress.
evidence.explanation: Names the complementary metabolic pathway that bypasses the block and notes its hepatic limitation. Evidence source is OTHER because this is the paper's background statement about human patients.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Dietary mannose is converted to mannose-6-phosphate by hexokinase, re-supplying the GDP-mannose pool without requiring MPI activity.

evidence.snippet: Patients with confirmed hyperinsulinaemia and hypoglycaemia might additionally need diazoxide treatment (reported doses vary from 4 to 15 mg/kg/day divided to three doses). The diazoxide is contraindicated in pregnancy.
evidence.explanation: Consensus recommendation with dose and the pregnancy contraindication.

treatments/1.description: Patients with confirmed hyperinsulinism and hypoglycaemia not controlled by mannose and feeding measures may need diazoxide, at reported doses of 4-15 mg/kg/day in three divided doses. Diazoxide is contraindicated in pregnancy.

evidence.snippet: In case of thrombosis, treatment by unfractionated heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin can be used.
evidence.explanation: Consensus first-line anticoagulation recommendation.

evidence.snippet: Infusion of factor XI concentrate or recombinant factor VIIa (rFVIIa) is not recommended due to the high risk of thrombotic events caused by unbalanced haemostasis.
evidence.explanation: Records the explicit agents-to-avoid recommendation for bleeding management.

evidence.snippet: Immediately after diagnosis of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, therapy with unfractionated heparin was initiated and changed to low molecular weight heparin 2 weeks later.
evidence.explanation: Worked clinical example of the anticoagulation strategy.

treatments/2.description: Thrombosis is treated with unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin. Vitamin K antagonists require caution because of bleeding risk in the setting of digestive ulceration and oesophageal varices, and factor XI concentrate and recombinant factor VIIa are not recommended because unbalanced haemostasis makes thrombosis likely.

evidence.snippet: Experimental heparin treatment of severe PLE was described in patient with serious adverse reactions after mannose.
evidence.explanation: Single-patient experimental use, reported descriptively by the guideline rather than as an established therapy.

treatments/3.description: Experimental heparin therapy has been used for severe protein-losing enteropathy in a patient with serious adverse reactions to mannose, on the rationale that heparin binds inflammatory cytokines that damage intestinal tight junctions. The bleeding risk in patients with coagulopathy, portal hypertension or varices must be weighed against the benefit; this is not routine disease-modifying treatment.

evidence.snippet: After transplantation her physical exercise tolerance, pulmonary functions, and metabolic parameters became fully restored.
evidence.explanation: Reports the first successful liver transplantation in a CDG patient.

evidence.snippet: Liver transplantation has been performed in one patient and could be necessary in selected cases (such as in patients with hepatopulmonary syndrome due to portal hypertension).
evidence.explanation: Consensus positioning of transplantation as a selected-case option.

treatments/4.description: Liver transplantation has been performed in selected patients, notably for hepatopulmonary syndrome secondary to portal hypertension. It restored exercise tolerance, pulmonary function, coagulation parameters and the transferrin isoelectric focusing pattern, although MPI enzyme activity and glycosylation of non-liver-derived glycoproteins remained deficient.

evidence.snippet: At presentation, severely undernourished patients with chronic diarrhoea or recurrent vomiting may require parenteral nutrition.
evidence.explanation: Consensus recommendation for nutritional rescue at presentation.

evidence.snippet: Hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia can be also managed by frequent feedings and by adding complex carbohydrates to the diet.
evidence.explanation: Consensus dietary management of the endocrine arm.

treatments/5.description: Severely undernourished patients with chronic diarrhoea or recurrent vomiting may need parenteral nutrition, nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding at presentation, and intravenous albumin before mannose achieves biochemical correction. Frequent feeds and complex dietary carbohydrate also help control hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia.

evidence.snippet: IV or SC immunoglobulins should be administered regularly in patients with hypogammaglobulinaemia.
evidence.explanation: Consensus recommendation for immunoglobulin replacement in the PLE-associated hypogammaglobulinaemia of MPI-CDG.

treatments/6.description: Patients with significant hypogammaglobulinaemia secondary to protein-losing enteropathy should receive regular intravenous or subcutaneous immunoglobulin replacement.

evidence.snippet: To the best of our knowledge, all the patients have liver involvement even at minimal stage, so the liver tests (transaminases, GGT, bilirubin, alpha-fetoprotein, prothrombin time) and liver ultrasound (in search for liver fibrosis, steatosis, ductal plate malformations, or signs of portal hypertension) should be performed every 6 months.
evidence.explanation: Consensus hepatic surveillance schedule, justified by the near-universal liver involvement.

evidence.snippet: Broad haemostatic study including fibrinogen, prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, factor VIII, factor IX, factor XI, AT, PC, and PS, complete blood count and differential should be performed at diagnosis and then annually.
evidence.explanation: Consensus haemostasis surveillance schedule.

evidence.snippet: oesophageal endoscopy should be performed each year at the beginning of the follow-up and thereafter depending on the endoscopic findings, but at least every 3 years.
evidence.explanation: Consensus variceal-surveillance interval for patients with portal hypertension.

treatments/7.description: Because the hepatic arm progresses independently of mannose and the coagulopathy fluctuates with intercurrent illness, the consensus guideline specifies scheduled surveillance rather than symptom-driven review: six-monthly liver chemistry (transaminases, GGT, bilirubin, alpha-fetoprotein, prothrombin time) plus liver ultrasound; annual elastography where transaminases remain elevated; annual and then at least three-yearly oesophageal endoscopy once portal hypertension is present, with echocardiography and oximetry for portopulmonary hypertension and hepatopulmonary syndrome; a broad annual haemostasis panel, repeated around infection, dehydration and any invasive procedure; albumin at a frequency set by the presence and severity of protein-losing enteropathy and the treatment response; and glucose, thyroid/IGF-axis, renal, immunoglobulin and nutritional review.

evidence.snippet: As the liver involvement in MPI-CDG is irreversible and progressive, the further liver damage should be prevented by vaccination against hepatotropic viruses (hepatitises A and B), avoidance of hepatotoxic drugs, and alcohol abstinence.
evidence.explanation: Consensus "agents and circumstances to avoid" recommendation.

treatments/8.description: Because the hepatic lesion is irreversible and progressive and unresponsive to mannose, further liver injury should be actively prevented: vaccination against hepatitis A and B, avoidance of hepatotoxic drugs, and abstinence from alcohol.

evidence.snippet: The identification of disease-causing variants enables accurate prenatal diagnosis, determination of carrier status of family members, and genetic counselling.
evidence.explanation: Consensus recommendation for genetic counselling following molecular diagnosis.

treatments/9.description: Identification of the causative variants supports carrier testing of family members, prenatal diagnosis and genetic counselling; psychological support for families is also recommended at the time of diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: However, the exact cause of HH in CDG patients is still unknown.
evidence.explanation: The consensus panel states the mechanism is unresolved.

open_questions/0.rationale: Hyperinsulinism accounts for more than two-thirds of hypoglycaemia in MPI-CDG and also occurs in PGM1-CDG and PMM2-CDG, suggesting a shared glycosylation-dependent mechanism, but the consensus guideline states the cause is unknown. Hypoglycosylation of the sulfonylurea receptor SUR1 is proposed and altered insulin secretion has been shown in hypoglycosylated murine beta cells, but neither has been demonstrated in human MPI-CDG islets. Resolving this would clarify why mannose corrects the hypoglycaemia and whether beta-cell-directed therapy is ever needed beyond diazoxide.

evidence.snippet: It is unknown whether mannose is harmful to human fetuses during gestation; however, mothers who are at risk for having MPI-CDG children and who consume mannose during pregnancy hoping to benefit an affected fetus in utero should be cautious.
evidence.explanation: The authors themselves flag the translational uncertainty, which is exactly the mismatch recorded here.

open_questions/1.rationale: The direction of the mannose effect is species- and route-discordant. Complete Mpi ablation in mice is embryonic lethal and mannose hastens embryonic death; Mpi hypomorphic mice develop blindness on antenatal mannose. Yet in zebrafish mannose rescues the phenotype when given early, and in humans oral mannose is well tolerated and clearly beneficial, with normal pregnancies reported in treated women; human toxicity has been seen only with the intravenous route. Whether the murine antenatal toxicity has any human counterpart is unresolved and directly gates the guideline's cautious stance on mannose in pregnancy.

evidence.snippet: Although an immunodeficiency was very likely, the conventional immune function studies were normal.
evidence.explanation: The guideline itself flags the dissociation between the clinical infection burden and normal immune testing.

open_questions/2.rationale: The secondary IgG loss of protein-losing enteropathy explains hypogammaglobulinaemia but not the reported infection phenotype: the patient with the most striking unusual infections and the four patients with recurrent fever, leucocytosis and sepsis all had normal conventional immunological testing. Glycosylation-dependent immune dysfunction is known in other CDGs, so a primary MPI-specific immune defect is plausible but undemonstrated. No causal edge is drawn to this phenotype for that reason.

evidence.snippet: Mild tubular acidosis, nephromegaly, renal cysts, and severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy were described in sporadic cases; the connection with MPI-CDG is unclear.
evidence.explanation: The guideline states the causal connection is unresolved, which is the gap recorded here.

open_questions/3.rationale: Renal findings were noticed in six reviewed patients, but the consensus guideline explicitly states that their connection with MPI-CDG is unclear, and altered kidney function has separately been reported in an adult on long-term mannose. Because even the causal association - let alone a mechanism - is unresolved, no causal edge is drawn to this phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Here, we characterize four patients with isolated complex II deficiency caused by mutations in SDHA presenting with multisystem mitochondrial disease including Leigh syndrome (LS) and/or leukodystrophy.
evidence.explanation: Documents biallelic SDHA mutations as the cause of isolated complex II deficiency presenting as multisystem mitochondrial disease.

evidence.snippet: Western blotting and BN-PAGE studies confirmed decreased steady-state levels of the relevant SDH subunits and impairment of complex II assembly.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that SDH gene defects reduce SDH subunit levels and impair complex II assembly.

steps/1.description: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in SDHA reduce or destabilize the catalytic flavoprotein subunit of succinate dehydrogenase, lowering steady-state levels of assembled complex II and the amount of catalytically active enzyme in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

evidence.snippet: Complex II oxidizes succinate to fumarate in the Krebs cycle and is involved in the mitochondrial electron transport chain.
evidence.explanation: Defines the dual TCA-cycle and electron-transport role of complex II that is lost when SDHA is deficient. Evidence source is OTHER because this is a review.

evidence.snippet: The deleterious effect of the Arg to Trp substitution on the catalytic activity of SDH was observed in a SDH- yeast strain transformed with mutant Fp cDNA.
evidence.explanation: Functional yeast complementation shows the flavoprotein-subunit mutation reduces SDH catalytic activity.

steps/2.description: Deficient complex II activity impairs FAD-dependent oxidation of succinate to fumarate and the transfer of electrons through the SDHB iron-sulfur clusters to ubiquinone, disrupting the junction between the TCA cycle and the respiratory electron transport chain.

evidence.snippet: Genetic disorders of the mitochondrial respiratory chain are often characterized by hypotonia, growth retardation, cardiomyopathy, myopathy, neuropathy, organ failure, and metabolic derangement.
evidence.explanation: Describes the multisystem, high-energy-tissue phenotype produced by respiratory-chain bioenergetic failure. Evidence source is OTHER because this is a review.

steps/3.description: Reduced electron flux through the respiratory chain lowers oxidative phosphorylation and forces a shift to anaerobic glycolysis, elevating lactate and producing lactic acidosis. Energy-demanding post-mitotic tissues (brain, skeletal muscle, optic nerve, and sometimes heart) are preferentially affected, giving the characteristic Leigh-spectrum and multisystem phenotype.

evidence.snippet: We now report a mutation in the nuclear-encoded flavoprotein (Fp) subunit gene of the succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) in two siblings with complex II deficiency presenting as Leigh syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Documents SDHA (flavoprotein subunit) complex II deficiency presenting as Leigh syndrome (subacute necrotizing encephalopathy).

steps/4.description: Subacute necrotizing encephalopathy (Leigh syndrome), the most common presentation of SDHA complex II deficiency.

evidence.snippet: we present the association of a mutation in the SDHA gene with recessive neonatal isolated DCM in 15 patients of two large consanguineous Bedouin families.
evidence.explanation: Documents recessive SDHA variants causing neonatal isolated dilated cardiomyopathy.

steps/5.description: Dilated cardiomyopathy from cardiomyocyte energy failure; can present in the neonatal period.

edges/1.description: Reduced active complex II lowers succinate:ubiquinone oxidoreductase capacity.

edges/2.description: Loss of succinate-driven electron flow reduces oxidative ATP synthesis.

edges/3.description: Energy deficit in brainstem and basal ganglia produces the necrotizing Leigh lesions.

edges/4.description: Chronic bioenergetic failure in cardiomyocytes drives cardiomyopathy in a subset of patients.
