evidence.explanation: Short stature occurred in 85.7% of this 42-patient referral cohort, mapping to VERY_FREQUENT; the population context is retained in the explanation rather than treated as a universal disease-wide estimate.

edges/15.description: Reduced transcription of intestinal VDR targets impairs active mineral absorption.

edges/16.description: Reduced VDR output dysregulates receptor-mediated vitamin D homeostasis, contributing to elevated calcitriol despite deficient biological action.

edges/17.description: Reduced active intestinal calcium uptake can lower circulating calcium.

edges/18.description: Reduced calcium delivery stimulates compensatory parathyroid hormone secretion even when that compensation maintains serum calcium near normal.

edges/19.description: Reduced calcium and phosphate delivery limits mineral substrate.

edges/22.description: Elevated PTH stimulates renal calcitriol production.

edges/24.description: Phosphate wasting further reduces substrate for hydroxyapatite deposition.

evidence.snippet: In each family, a different single nucleotide mutation was found in the DNA binding domain of the protein; one family near the tip of the first zinc finger (Gly----Asp) and one at the tip of the second zinc finger (Arg----Gly).
evidence.explanation: Identifies the causal VDR variants and localizes them to the DNA-binding domain.

evidence.snippet: Molecular genetic testing of the VDR gene in our cohort identified six different gene variants c.885 C>A (p.Tyr295Ter), c.88 C>T (p.Arg30Ter), c.1036G>A (p.Val346Met), c.820C>T (p.Arg274Cys), c.803 T>C (p.Ile268Thr), and c.2T>G (p.Met1?).
evidence.explanation: Documents the allelic spectrum in the largest reported cohort.

evidence.snippet: The mutant had a dominant-negative effect on wild-type-VDR, and the ligand binding affinity of Q400LfsX7-VDR was completely impaired.
evidence.explanation: Functional testing identifies Q400LfsX7 as a dominant-negative causal VDR allele rather than treating the accompanying functionally normal R370H variant as causal.

evidence.snippet: In conclusion, we describe a novel mutation, I268T, in the VDR ligand-binding domain that alters ligand binding, retinoid X receptor heterodimerization, and coactivator binding.
evidence.explanation: Establishes p.Ile268Thr as a ligand-binding-domain allele and documents its experimentally measured multiple functional defects.

evidence.snippet: We found that the child was homozygous for a unique missense mutation in the VDR gene that converted valine to methionine at amino acid 26 (V26M) in the VDR DNA-binding domain (DBD).
evidence.explanation: Provides a representative DNA-binding-domain missense allele.

evidence.snippet: A novel homozygous missense R343H mutation in the exon 9 of VDR residing in the retinoid X receptor (RXR)-binding domain was identified.
evidence.explanation: Provides the p.Arg343His example and its location at the RXR-binding interface.

evidence.snippet: Genetic testing using whole-exome sequencing identified a homozygous pathogenic variant in the VDR (c.1027C>T, p.R343C), confirming the diagnosis of VDDR2A. Both parents were found to be heterozygous carriers.
evidence.explanation: Provides the p.Arg343Cys example and recessive segregation.

evidence.snippet: The VDR c.1027C>T (p.R343C) variant results in a missense substitution of arginine, a polar amino acid, to cysteine, a neutral and slight polar amino acid, at position 343, which is located within the LBD of the VDR [12].
evidence.explanation: Locally establishes p.Arg343Cys as an LBD allele without inferring a specific interface defect or functional consequence from this case.

evidence.snippet: Several types of variants have been identified in the VDR gene as the leading cause of HVDDR-II, such as non-sense, substitutions, insertions, duplications, deletions, and splice-site (2).
evidence.explanation: Documents the broad causal variant classes, including splice-site alleles.

evidence.snippet: In summary, we describe a patient with compound heterozygous mutations in the VDR that results in HVDRR with alopecia.
evidence.explanation: Establishes compound heterozygosity as a disease-causing allelic state.

evidence.snippet: This is the first report of HVDRR caused by UPD, and the third case of complete UPD of chromosome 12, in the published literature.
evidence.explanation: Separates the exceptional route to homozygosity from the usual biparental recessive inheritance.

genes/0.notes: Most affected individuals have homozygous or compound-heterozygous VDR variants; complete maternal chromosome-12 isodisomy is a rare alternative route to homozygosity. Representative alleles span non-truncating ligand-binding-domain variants such as p.Ile268Thr and p.Arg343Cys, DNA-binding-domain variants such as p.Val26Met, the RXR-binding-domain p.Arg343His variant, splice-site variants, truncating variants, and compound-heterozygous combinations. Functional consequences include absent or truncated receptor, impaired ligand binding, impaired DNA binding, defective RXR heterodimerization, and defective coactivator recruitment; residual activity, alopecia, and treatment response vary by allele class. Exceptionally, heterozygous dominant-negative alleles such as p.Q400LfsX7 inhibit wild-type VDR through constitutive corepressor retention and cause dominant disease.

treatments/0.description: Patients with residual VDR responsiveness, particularly some non-truncating ligand-binding-domain variants and milder presentations without alopecia, may respond to supraphysiologic calcitriol or alfacalcidol together with oral calcium. Biochemical response, growth, and radiographic healing guide continued use; response cannot be inferred from alopecia alone.

evidence.snippet: High-dose calcitriol therapy resulted in progressive biochemical improvement and catch-up growth.
evidence.explanation: Genetically confirmed p.R343C VDDR2A responded clinically and biochemically, disproving universal calcitriol nonresponse.

evidence.snippet: Overall response to oral therapy was highest in LBD-NT (46.4%) as compared to 7.6% in LBD-truncating and 19% in DBD-NT variants.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies genotype-stratified oral response and supports a response-guided rather than universal treatment claim.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Supraphysiologic active vitamin D can increase signaling through a receptor with residual function.

evidence.snippet: They both are being managed on high doses of oral calcium supplements and activated form of vitamin D.
evidence.explanation: Documents oral calcium plus activated vitamin D management in two genetically characterized siblings.

treatments/0/targets/1.description: High oral calcium concentrations increase passive calcium uptake while active vitamin D exploits any residual receptor activity.

treatments/1.description: High-dose oral elemental calcium is an initial bypass strategy when it can restore normocalcemia and suppress secondary hyperparathyroidism. It may also permit transition away from intravenous calcium, but passive absorption is limited and requires close biochemical and urinary-calcium monitoring.

evidence.snippet: Management during the first few months of life may require only administration of high doses of oral calcium (5–6 g/m2 body surface of elemental calcium). If oral therapy is able to restore normocalcemia and reverse secondary hyperparathyroidism it may not be necessary to initiate intravenous infusions of calcium.
evidence.explanation: Supports oral-first calcium treatment when biochemical targets respond.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: A large luminal calcium load increases VDR-independent passive absorption.

treatments/2.description: Severe disease that fails maximal oral calcium and active vitamin D requires prolonged intravenous calcium to bypass intestinal absorption entirely and replenish skeletal calcium deficits. Central-line complications make this a refractory-disease strategy, not evidence that intravenous therapy is universally preferable.

evidence.snippet: Those patients who fail to respond to maximal doses of calciferol will require intravenous infusions of calcium (1,000 mg elemental calcium per 24 h infused over 12 h), which can be used even by the youngest children with VDDR2a.
evidence.explanation: Restricts intravenous calcium to patients who fail maximal hormone-based treatment.

evidence.snippet: All patients had poor overall response to oral high-dose calcium and calcitriol and most required intravenous calcium.
evidence.explanation: Documents escalation to intravenous calcium in an oral-refractory genetically confirmed cohort.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Intravenous delivery completely bypasses the receptor-dependent intestinal route.

evidence.snippet: Wiedemann‐Steiner syndrome (WSS) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by monoallelic variants in KMT2A and characterized by intellectual disability and hypertrichosis.
evidence.explanation: The 104-person cohort confirms monoallelic KMT2A variants as causal.

evidence.snippet: Haploinsufficiency of mixed-lineage leukemia (MLL/KMT2A) protein causes Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome (WSS), a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with microcephaly.
evidence.explanation: The mechanistic study identifies KMT2A haploinsufficiency as the upstream disease lesion.

steps/1.description: The initiating lesion is reduced KMT2A function from a heterozygous pathogenic variant. KMT2A encodes an H3K4 methyltransferase, but the clinical allelic spectrum is not limited to experimentally proven loss-of-function variants; the causal statement is therefore kept at the gene-disease level.

evidence.snippet: the here-described WSS patients demonstrated a block in terminal B cell differentiation evidenced by a relative increase in transitional and naive B cells and a relative decrease in switched memory B cells
evidence.explanation: Direct immunophenotyping evidence for the terminal B-cell differentiation block in KMT2A-mutated individuals.

evidence.snippet: all patients from families A and B had decreased circulating follicular helper T (cTfh) cells
evidence.explanation: Establishes the reduced circulating follicular helper T-cell compartment that accompanies the B-cell block.

evidence.snippet: KMT2A deficiency (Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome) KMT2A AD 605130
evidence.explanation: The IUIS expert committee lists KMT2A deficiency as an inborn error of immunity, with hypogammaglobulinemia and decreased memory B cells as the recorded immunologic phenotype.

steps/2.description: The immunologic arm of WDSTS, and the reason IUIS lists KMT2A deficiency among the combined immunodeficiencies with syndromic features. Detailed immunophenotyping of a KMT2A-mutated kindred showed a block in terminal B-cell differentiation - relatively increased transitional and naive B cells with relatively decreased switched memory B cells - accompanied by reduced circulating follicular helper T cells, which are required for germinal-centre help. The result is panhypogammaglobulinemia with poor polysaccharide vaccine responses. Whether the B-cell block is B-cell intrinsic or secondary to the T-follicular-helper deficit is unresolved, and the observations rest on a small number of reported families.

evidence.snippet: In western blot analyses, global H3K4me1–3 levels were not altered dramatically in any mutant
evidence.explanation: This negative result prevents overinterpreting KMT2A haploinsufficiency as a global H3K4 methylation deficiency.

evidence.snippet: By relaxing the threshold, we obtained weak 2A-HET DMRs
evidence.explanation: The reported Kmt2a-heterozygous H3K4me3 changes were weak and locus-specific, supporting the deliberately qualified node.

steps/3.description: KMT2A is an H3K4 methylation writer and transcriptional coactivator. In adult Kmt2a-heterozygous mouse brain, transcriptional changes and weak locus-specific H3K4me3 differences were detected, while global H3K4me1-3 levels were not dramatically altered. This supports locus- and cell-context-dependent dysregulation rather than a proven global histone methylation loss. The genome-wide DNA methylation episignature used diagnostically is a distinct measurement and is not evidence of reduced histone H3K4 methylation.

evidence.snippet: Despite opposite enzymatic activities, the two mouse models deficient for either Kmt2a or Kdm5c shared reduced dendritic spines and increased aggression. Double mutation of Kmt2a and Kdm5c clearly reversed dendritic morphology, key behavioral traits including aggression, and partially corrected altered transcriptomes and H3K4me landscapes.
evidence.explanation: The study links Kmt2a deficiency to dendritic and behavioral changes in a mouse model, while its human translational relevance remains unproven.

steps/4.description: Constitutive Kmt2a-heterozygous mice show reduced dendritic spine density and increased aggression. Combining Kmt2a heterozygosity with Kdm5c deficiency reversed dendritic morphology and key behavioral traits and partially corrected transcriptomic and H3K4me changes. These observations support a neuronal branch but have not yet been confirmed in human developmental neurons.

evidence.snippet: Loss of the MLL/WDR5 complex affects microtubule nucleation and regrowth. MLL/WDR5 localize to the pericentriolar material and interact with centriolar satellite protein Cep72 and γ-tubulin ring complex proteins (γ-TuRCs).
evidence.explanation: The study demonstrates a non-nuclear MLL/WDR5-Cep72 centrosomal function and reports the phenotype in WSS-derived cells.

steps/5.description: The MLL/WDR5 complex localizes to pericentriolar material, interacts with Cep72 and gamma-tubulin ring-complex proteins, and promotes centrosomal recruitment of structural proteins. Loss of MLL/WDR5 impairs microtubule nucleation and spindle formation; a related localization phenotype was also observed in cells derived from people with WSS. How much this branch contributes to the human neurodevelopmental phenotype remains uncertain.

evidence.snippet: Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome (WSS) is characterized by developmental delay, intellectual disability, and characteristic facial features, with or without additional congenital anomalies.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews identifies characteristic facial features as one of the core clinical findings.

steps/6.description: Characteristic facial features are a defining part of the WDSTS phenotype. Reported features include thick eyebrows with lateral flare, vertically narrow downslanting palpebral fissures, widely spaced eyes, a wide nasal bridge, broad nasal tip, thin upper-lip vermilion, and thick scalp hair.

evidence.snippet: Fifty-seven percent of children diagnosed with WSS have hypotonia, and 90% have developmental delay.
evidence.explanation: The review's developmental-delay estimate directly supports the very-frequent frequency band.

evidence.snippet: Common clinical features identified in the cohort included: developmental delay or intellectual disability (97%), constipation (63.8%), failure to thrive (67.7%), feeding difficulties (66.3%), hypertrichosis cubiti (57%), short stature (57.8%), and vertebral anomalies (46.9%).
evidence.explanation: The Sheppard et al. n=104 multi-centre cohort provides the most robust frequency estimate (97%) for developmental delay/intellectual disability in WDSTS.

evidence.snippet: The median ages at walking and first words were 20 months and 18 months, respectively.
evidence.explanation: The same cohort quantifies delayed motor and speech milestones.

steps/7.description: Developmental delay was reported in 90% of affected children in a physical-therapy review, while developmental delay or intellectual disability combined was reported in 97% of the largest cohort. Median ages at first words and independent walking were 18 and 20 months, respectively, demonstrating delays across communication and motor milestones.

evidence.snippet: The majority of patients performed in the below average to very low ranges in Nonverbal Reasoning, Visual/Spatial Perception, Visuoconstruction, Visual Memory, Attention, Working Memory and Math Computation skills. In contrast, over half the sample performed within normal limits on Receptive Vocabulary, Verbal Memory, and Word Reading.
evidence.explanation: Ng et al. characterise the specific neurocognitive profile of WSS in 10 patients; the small sample supports a profile description but not a population-wide severity distribution.

evidence.snippet: Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome (WSS) is characterized by developmental delay, intellectual disability, and characteristic facial features, with or without additional congenital anomalies.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews identifies intellectual disability as a core clinical feature.

steps/8.description: Intellectual disability is a core feature of WDSTS, although severity is variable. In a neuropsychological series of ten molecularly confirmed children, nonverbal reasoning, visuospatial skills, visual memory, attention, working memory, and mathematics were often weaker than receptive vocabulary, verbal memory, and word reading.

evidence.snippet: Fifty-seven percent of children diagnosed with WSS have hypotonia, and 90% have developmental delay. The diagnosis of WSS should require physical therapy services through early intervention programs due to its high correlation with motor developmental delay and disability.
evidence.explanation: Mendoza 2020 reports a 57% frequency estimate and connects hypotonia with the need for early motor intervention.

evidence.snippet: Hypotonia was associated with loss of function (LoF) variants, and seizures were associated with non‐LoF variants.
evidence.explanation: Sheppard et al. identify a genotype-phenotype correlation: hypotonia is specifically associated with loss-of-function KMT2A variants.

steps/9.description: Hypotonia was reported in 57% of affected children in a physical-therapy review and was associated with loss-of-function KMT2A variants in the 104-person cohort. It commonly accompanies motor developmental delay.

evidence.snippet: Common clinical features identified in the cohort included: developmental delay or intellectual disability (97%), constipation (63.8%), failure to thrive (67.7%), feeding difficulties (66.3%), hypertrichosis cubiti (57%), short stature (57.8%), and vertebral anomalies (46.9%).
evidence.explanation: Short stature is present in 57.8% of the Sheppard multi-centre cohort of 104 individuals.

evidence.snippet: The most common clinical features were short stature (90.9%) and developmental delay (90.9%), followed by intellectual disability (72.7%).
evidence.explanation: Lin et al. report short stature as the most frequent feature (90.9%) in a Chinese cohort, emphasising cross-ethnic variability in phenotype frequency.

steps/10.description: Short stature was reported in 57.8% of the 104-person international cohort and in 90.9% of a smaller cohort of 11 Chinese children. The difference illustrates ascertainment and cohort variability rather than an established population range.

evidence.snippet: Common clinical features identified in the cohort included: developmental delay or intellectual disability (97%), constipation (63.8%), failure to thrive (67.7%), feeding difficulties (66.3%), hypertrichosis cubiti (57%), short stature (57.8%), and vertebral anomalies (46.9%).
evidence.explanation: Hypertrichosis cubiti is present in 57% of the n=104 cohort, confirming it as a frequent but not invariant hallmark of WDSTS.

evidence.snippet: Hypertrichosis cubiti that was supposed to be pathognomonic in the literature was found only in 61% of our cases.
evidence.explanation: Baer et al. report hypertrichosis cubiti in 61% of 33 French WDSTS cases, noting it is not pathognomonic—molecular diagnosis is required.

steps/11.description: Hypertrichosis, particularly involving the elbows (hypertrichosis cubiti), is a hallmark feature of WDSTS, reported in 57% of the 104-person cohort and 61% of a 33-person French cohort. It is therefore frequent but neither invariant nor sufficient for diagnosis; hypertrichosis of other body regions may also occur.

evidence.snippet: Common clinical features identified in the cohort included: developmental delay or intellectual disability (97%), constipation (63.8%), failure to thrive (67.7%), feeding difficulties (66.3%), hypertrichosis cubiti (57%), short stature (57.8%), and vertebral anomalies (46.9%).
evidence.explanation: Feeding difficulties are present in 66.3% of the n=104 cohort, making it one of the most frequent gastrointestinal features of WDSTS.

evidence.snippet: Feeding therapy with possible supplemental tube feeding for those with poor weight gain / failure to thrive
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews directly supports feeding therapy and selective tube feeding when poor growth persists.

steps/12.description: Feeding difficulties were reported in 66.3% of the 104-person cohort and can accompany poor weight gain or failure to thrive. GeneReviews recommends feeding therapy and, when needed, supplemental tube feeding.

evidence.snippet: Common clinical features identified in the cohort included: developmental delay or intellectual disability (97%), constipation (63.8%), failure to thrive (67.7%), feeding difficulties (66.3%), hypertrichosis cubiti (57%), short stature (57.8%), and vertebral anomalies (46.9%).
evidence.explanation: Failure to thrive is present in 67.7% of the n=104 Sheppard cohort.

steps/13.description: Failure to thrive was reported in 67.7% of the 104-person cohort and is a common clinical management concern, particularly when feeding difficulties and poor weight gain occur together.

evidence.snippet: Common clinical features identified in the cohort included: developmental delay or intellectual disability (97%), constipation (63.8%), failure to thrive (67.7%), feeding difficulties (66.3%), hypertrichosis cubiti (57%), short stature (57.8%), and vertebral anomalies (46.9%).
evidence.explanation: Constipation is present in 63.8% of the n=104 cohort, making it the most common gastrointestinal comorbidity in WDSTS after feeding difficulties.

evidence.snippet: At each visit: measurement of growth parameters; evaluation of nutritional status; assessment for constipation
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews includes constipation assessment in routine surveillance.

steps/14.description: Constipation was reported in 63.8% of the 104-person cohort. GeneReviews recommends assessment at clinical visits and standard bowel management when present; a syndrome-specific cause has not been established.

evidence.snippet: Most caregivers reported deficits in executive functioning, most notably in emotion regulation.
evidence.explanation: Ng et al. identify executive function and emotion regulation deficits as a characteristic behavioural feature of WDSTS in a neuropsychological case series of 10 patients.

steps/15.description: Behavioral and executive-function differences occur in WDSTS. In a neuropsychological series of ten children, most caregivers reported executive difficulties, particularly emotion regulation. The small series does not establish a population frequency or a uniform behavioral profile.

evidence.snippet: Common clinical features identified in the cohort included: developmental delay or intellectual disability (97%), constipation (63.8%), failure to thrive (67.7%), feeding difficulties (66.3%), hypertrichosis cubiti (57%), short stature (57.8%), and vertebral anomalies (46.9%).
evidence.explanation: Vertebral anomalies are among the most common structural comorbidities in WDSTS, present in 46.9% of the n=104 multi-centre cohort.

evidence.snippet: Cervical spine anomalies may lead to immobility or instability, which may complicate airway management. Vertebral anomalies or scoliosis in the thoracic or lumbar spine may complicate spinal or epidural anesthesia.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews states the anesthesia implications of cervical and thoracolumbar vertebral disease.

steps/16.description: Vertebral anomalies were reported in 46.9% of the 104-person cohort, with fusion anomalies of the cervical spine specifically recognized in GeneReviews. Cervical and thoracolumbar abnormalities can have implications for airway, spinal, or epidural anesthesia planning.

evidence.snippet: Vertebral anomalies or scoliosis in the thoracic or lumbar spine may complicate spinal or epidural anesthesia.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews explicitly documents scoliosis and thoracolumbar vertebral anomalies as clinically significant features in WDSTS, with anesthesia implications.

steps/17.description: Scoliosis is a recognized musculoskeletal manifestation of WDSTS. It can coexist with other vertebral anomalies and may complicate spinal or epidural anesthesia; the cited summary does not provide a reliable population frequency.

evidence.snippet: Hypotonia was associated with loss of function (LoF) variants, and seizures were associated with non‐LoF variants.
evidence.explanation: Sheppard et al. report an association between seizures and non-LoF KMT2A variants without quantifying it in the abstract.

evidence.snippet: Other clinical features include feeding difficulties, prenatal and postnatal growth restriction, epilepsy, ophthalmologic anomalies, congenital heart defects
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews includes epilepsy among the recognized clinical features.

steps/18.description: Epilepsy is a recognized but variably present feature of WDSTS. In the 104-person cohort, seizures were associated with non-loss-of-function KMT2A variants. The cited abstract does not provide a population frequency.

evidence.snippet: The most frequent imaging features were patent ductus arteriosus (57.1%) and patent foramen ovale (42.9%) in cardiovascular system, and abnormal corpus callosum (50.0%) in the brain.
evidence.explanation: Lin et al. quantify PDA and PFO within a small Chinese imaging cohort.

evidence.snippet: ophthalmologic anomalies, congenital heart defects, hand anomalies
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews confirms congenital heart defects as part of the clinical spectrum.

steps/19.description: Congenital heart defects are part of the WDSTS spectrum. In a cohort of 11 Chinese children, the most frequent cardiovascular imaging findings among those evaluated were patent ductus arteriosus (57.1%) and patent foramen ovale (42.9%); these cohort-specific figures should not be generalized.

evidence.snippet: The most frequent imaging features were patent ductus arteriosus (57.1%) and patent foramen ovale (42.9%) in cardiovascular system, and abnormal corpus callosum (50.0%) in the brain.
evidence.explanation: Lin et al. report abnormal corpus callosum morphology in the imaging subset of their 11-person Chinese cohort.

steps/20.description: Brain malformations are part of the WDSTS spectrum. Abnormal corpus callosum morphology was reported in 50% of the imaged subset of a small Chinese cohort; this figure is cohort-specific and its relationship to cognitive outcomes has not been established.

evidence.snippet: Other clinical features include feeding difficulties, prenatal and postnatal growth restriction, epilepsy, ophthalmologic anomalies, congenital heart defects, hand anomalies (such as brachydactyly and clinodactyly), hypotonia, vertebral anomalies (especially fusion anomalies of the cervical spine), renal and uterine anomalies, immune dysfunction, brain malformations, and dental anomalies.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents ophthalmologic anomalies as a recognised clinical feature of WDSTS; ophthalmologic evaluation annually is recommended.

steps/21.description: Ophthalmologic anomalies are recognized in WDSTS. GeneReviews recommends standard management of eye anomalies and periodic ophthalmologic assessment, but the cited summary does not define the distribution or population frequency of specific eye findings.

evidence.snippet: CPAP, BiPAP, or surgical removal of the tonsils and adenoids for those with obstructive sleep apnea
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews includes CPAP/BiPAP and surgical adenotonsillectomy as management for OSA in WDSTS, confirming it as a recognised clinical feature warranting active screening.

steps/22.description: Obstructive sleep apnea is a recognized treatable manifestation in WDSTS. GeneReviews lists CPAP, BiPAP, and surgical removal of the tonsils and adenoids as management options; the cited summary does not establish its frequency or a syndrome-specific cause.

evidence.snippet: consideration of IVIG therapy in those with low antibody levels; consideration of prophylactic antibiotics in those with frequent infections
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends IVIG and prophylactic antibiotics for WDSTS individuals with immune dysfunction, confirming recurrent infections as a clinically significant and manageable comorbidity.

evidence.snippet: From the first year of life, the twin boys suffered from recurrent upper and lower respiratory tract infections, often requiring antibiotics.
evidence.explanation: Documents the recurrent sinopulmonary infection pattern in a molecularly confirmed KMT2A kindred.

evidence.snippet: Respiratory infections; short stature; hypertelorism; hairy elbows; developmental delay, intellectual disability
evidence.explanation: The IUIS Table 2 row for KMT2A deficiency records respiratory infections alongside the syndromic features.

steps/23.description: Immune dysfunction and recurrent infections occur in some individuals with WDSTS, and are the reason KMT2A deficiency appears in the IUIS inborn errors of immunity classification. The dominant infectious pattern in the reported KMT2A kindreds is recurrent upper and lower respiratory tract infection from early childhood, sometimes progressing to bronchiectasis. GeneReviews recommends considering IVIG for low antibody levels and prophylactic antibiotics for frequent infections; neither the GeneReviews summary nor the reported case series supports a population frequency.

evidence.snippet: Upon immunological evaluation, both patients II:2 and II:3 demonstrated panhypogammaglobulinemia, poor antibody responses to Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine, increased naive B cells, and very low memory B cells
evidence.explanation: Documents panhypogammaglobulinemia in two molecularly confirmed KMT2A siblings.

evidence.snippet: we report on a boy with a complex phenotype overlapping WSS but exhibiting epilepsy, feeding difficulties, microcephaly, and congenital immunodeficiency with low levels of immunoglobulins as additional features
evidence.explanation: An independent case report of low immunoglobulins with a de novo KMT2A missense variant.

evidence.snippet: KMT2A deficiency (Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome) KMT2A AD 605130
evidence.explanation: The IUIS Table 2 row records hypogammaglobulinemia with decreased antibody responses as the associated serum immunoglobulin phenotype.

steps/24.description: Reduced serum immunoglobulin concentrations are the central laboratory abnormality of the WDSTS immune phenotype and the basis of the IUIS listing. Reported individuals have shown panhypogammaglobulinemia, and a separate case report described congenital immunodeficiency with low immunoglobulins. Presentation can precede recognition of the syndromic features, so an early-onset CVID-like picture may be the presenting problem. The reported series are too small to support a frequency.

evidence.snippet: the here-described WSS patients demonstrated a block in terminal B cell differentiation evidenced by a relative increase in transitional and naive B cells and a relative decrease in switched memory B cells
evidence.explanation: Directly documents the reduced switched memory B-cell compartment in KMT2A-mutated individuals.

evidence.snippet: Subsequent investigations in the mother demonstrated mild intellectual disability, undetectable serum IgM, and reduced switched memory B cells
evidence.explanation: Shows the same B-cell abnormality in the mildly affected transmitting parent.

steps/25.description: A reduced proportion of class-switched (IgD-CD27+) memory B cells, with a relative expansion of transitional and naive B cells, is the cellular signature of the WDSTS antibody deficiency. The same pattern was found in an affected mother identified only after her children were diagnosed, indicating it can be present in mildly affected carriers. IUIS records both switched and non-switched memory B-cell compartments as decreased.

evidence.snippet: poor antibody responses to Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine
evidence.explanation: Documents the impaired polysaccharide vaccine response in KMT2A-mutated siblings.

steps/26.description: Poor antibody responses to unconjugated pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine were documented in molecularly confirmed KMT2A cases, and IUIS records decreased antibody responses as part of the KMT2A deficiency immunologic phenotype. This is the functional counterpart of the reduced switched memory B-cell compartment and is what distinguishes the finding from an isolated low immunoglobulin measurement.

evidence.snippet: Other clinical features include feeding difficulties, prenatal and postnatal growth restriction, epilepsy, ophthalmologic anomalies, congenital heart defects, hand anomalies (such as brachydactyly and clinodactyly), hypotonia, vertebral anomalies (especially fusion anomalies of the cervical spine), renal and uterine anomalies, immune dysfunction, brain malformations, and dental anomalies.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists renal and uterine anomalies as recognized clinical features of WDSTS.

steps/27.description: Renal and uterine anomalies are recognized manifestations of WDSTS, with additional genitourinary findings reported in cohorts. The cited GeneReviews summary does not provide a frequency or justify a single aggregate estimate for all genitourinary anomalies.

evidence.snippet: hand anomalies (such as brachydactyly and clinodactyly)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews explicitly lists brachydactyly and clinodactyly among the clinical manifestations.

steps/28.description: Hand anomalies, especially brachydactyly and clinodactyly, are recognized components of the WDSTS phenotype. Available summary evidence establishes their presence but does not provide a reliable population frequency.

evidence.snippet: brain malformations, and dental anomalies.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews includes dental anomalies in the clinical spectrum.

steps/29.description: Dental anomalies are part of the variable multisystem WDSTS phenotype. The available GeneReviews summary establishes their presence but does not define a syndrome-specific pattern or population frequency.

evidence.snippet: growth hormone therapy for those with growth hormone deficiency; thyroid replacement therapy for hypothyroidism
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews explicitly recommends growth hormone therapy when growth hormone deficiency is present.

steps/30.description: Growth hormone deficiency occurs in a subset of individuals with WDSTS and is clinically relevant because growth hormone therapy may be considered when the deficiency is confirmed. The cited summary does not provide a population frequency.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show functional interactions of a writer-eraser duo, KMT2A and KDM5C, which are responsible for Wiedemann-Steiner Syndrome (WDSTS), and mental retardation X-linked syndromic Claes-Jensen type (MRXSCJ), respectively.
evidence.explanation: This mouse study supports an H3K4 writer/eraser relationship, but not a uniform global methylation-loss model in human disease.

edges/1.description: Reduced activity of the H3K4 writer KMT2A can alter H3K4 methylation and transcription at selected loci; available mouse data do not show a simple global reduction in H3K4 methylation.

evidence.snippet: Loss of the MLL/WDR5 complex affects microtubule nucleation and regrowth.
evidence.explanation: Direct depletion experiments link loss of the MLL/WDR5 complex to defective microtubule nucleation.

evidence.snippet: Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome (WSS) is characterized by developmental delay, intellectual disability, and characteristic facial features, with or without additional congenital anomalies.
evidence.explanation: Characteristic facial features are part of molecularly defined WDSTS; the intervening developmental pathway is not established.

edges/17.description: Reduced KMT2A function is associated with a block in terminal B-cell differentiation and consequent antibody deficiency. The molecular route from KMT2A dosage to the B-cell phenotype has not been established.

evidence.snippet: growth hormone therapy for those with growth hormone deficiency

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous pathogenic KMT2A variants cause WDSTS. The allelic spectrum is highly heterogeneous: 69 of 82 variants in the 104-person cohort were novel. Most tested families represent de novo disease, but vertical autosomal dominant transmission and parental mosaicism occur. In that cohort, hypotonia was associated with loss-of-function variants and seizures with non-loss-of-function variants; the abstract does not support more granular variant-class percentages or a universal functional mechanism.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of WSS should require physical therapy services through early intervention programs due to its high correlation with motor developmental delay and disability.
evidence.explanation: The physical-therapy report explicitly recommends early PT services for motor delay and disability.

treatments/0.description: Early physical therapy through developmental intervention programs addresses hypotonia, motor delay, mobility, and functional skills. Evidence specific to WDSTS is limited to case-based physical-therapy literature and expert management guidance.

evidence.snippet: standard treatment for epilepsy, developmental delay / intellectual disability
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews directly recommends standard management for developmental delay and intellectual disability.

treatments/1.description: Standard developmental management is recommended for developmental delay or intellectual disability. The cited guidance does not specify a syndrome-specific speech-language modality or treatment regimen.

evidence.snippet: The majority of patients performed in the below average to very low ranges in Nonverbal Reasoning, Visual/Spatial Perception, Visuoconstruction, Visual Memory, Attention, Working Memory and Math Computation skills.
evidence.explanation: The neuropsychological profile informs occupational-therapy targets but is not a treatment trial.

treatments/2.description: Occupational therapy addresses fine motor delays, visuospatial difficulties, activities of daily living, and adaptive needs. The reported nonverbal/visuospatial weaknesses can inform individualized goals; direct WDSTS-specific efficacy evidence is not available.

evidence.snippet: behavioral therapy; standard treatment for epilepsy, developmental delay / intellectual disability
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews directly recommends behavioral therapy.

treatments/3.description: Behavioral therapy and standard psychiatric care are used for clinically significant behavioral, attention, autistic, anxiety, or emotion-regulation concerns. Intervention should be based on the individual's presentation; no WDSTS-specific drug regimen is established in the cited guidance.

evidence.snippet: We observed autosomal dominant transmission of WSS in 3 families and mosaicism in one family.
evidence.explanation: Baer et al. document both familial transmission and mosaicism in French WDSTS cases, underscoring the importance of genetic counselling including parental testing.

evidence.snippet: Each offspring of an individual with WSS is at a 50% risk of being affected. Once the KMT2A pathogenic variant has been identified in an affected family member, prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing are possible.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews states the transmission risk and available reproductive testing options.

treatments/4.description: Counseling covers the typically de novo but autosomal dominant inheritance, the possibility of an affected or mosaic parent, the 50% transmission risk for an affected individual, and prenatal or preimplantation genetic testing once the familial KMT2A pathogenic variant is known.

evidence.snippet: Two patients were treated with rhGH and yielded satisfactory height gains, but one developed acceleration of bone age.
evidence.explanation: Lin et al. report rhGH use in two WDSTS patients with short stature, showing benefit but also bone age acceleration as a potential adverse effect.

evidence.snippet: growth hormone therapy for those with growth hormone deficiency
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews limits the recommendation to confirmed deficiency.

treatments/5.description: Recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) therapy has been trialled in WDSTS patients with short stature. In a Chinese cohort, two patients treated with rhGH showed satisfactory height gains, though one experienced acceleration of bone age. GeneReviews recommends treatment specifically for confirmed growth hormone deficiency; the two-person observation does not establish general efficacy for all WDSTS-associated short stature.

evidence.snippet: standard treatment for epilepsy, developmental delay / intellectual disability
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends standard epilepsy treatment rather than a syndrome-specific medication.

evidence.snippet: The authors are aware of one individual with WSS who developed hyperammonemia with the use of the anti-seizure medication valproate. While this is not specific to individuals with WSS, valproate should be used with caution.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews records the single hyperammonemia observation and qualifies the resulting valproate caution.

treatments/6.description: Epilepsy is treated according to standard neurologic practice; no WDSTS-specific antiseizure regimen is established. Valproate warrants caution because GeneReviews reports one affected individual who developed hyperammonemia, while explicitly noting that this event is not specific to WDSTS.

evidence.snippet: consideration of IVIG therapy in those with low antibody levels; consideration of prophylactic antibiotics in those with frequent infections
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends IVIG and prophylactic antibiotics as management for immune dysfunction in WDSTS.

evidence.snippet: we report two sibling pairs with syndromic primary immunodeficiencies that exceptionally presented with a phenotype resembling early-onset common variable immunodeficiency
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the antibody deficiency can be the presenting problem, which is what makes immunoglobulin replacement a first-line concern in some individuals.

treatments/7.description: For WDSTS individuals with documented low antibody levels or immune dysfunction, IVIG therapy is recommended. Prophylactic antibiotics should be considered for those with frequent infections. Immunological evaluation and infection history guide selection; these are conditional measures rather than routine treatment for every affected person. Because the antibody deficiency can present before the syndromic features are recognized, the reported kindreds were managed as common variable immunodeficiency for years before the KMT2A diagnosis was made.

evidence.snippet: consideration of IVIG therapy in those with low antibody levels

treatments/7/targets/0.description: Immunoglobulin replacement supplies antibody directly and so bypasses the failure of terminal B-cell differentiation rather than correcting it.

evidence.snippet: Feeding therapy with possible supplemental tube feeding for those with poor weight gain / failure to thrive
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews directly states both the feeding-therapy recommendation and conditional tube supplementation.

treatments/8.description: Feeding therapy is recommended for poor weight gain or failure to thrive, with supplemental tube feeding considered when oral strategies are insufficient. The approach is individualized to nutritional status and feeding safety.

evidence.snippet: stool softeners or osmotic agents for bowel dysfunction
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews specifies standard pharmacologic bowel management.

treatments/9.description: Bowel dysfunction is managed with standard measures such as stool softeners or osmotic agents, selected according to clinical assessment and response.

evidence.snippet: CPAP, BiPAP, or surgical removal of the tonsils and adenoids for those with obstructive sleep apnea
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists both noninvasive ventilation and surgical airway options.

treatments/10.description: Obstructive sleep apnea may be managed with CPAP or BiPAP, or with removal of the tonsils and adenoids when clinically indicated. Choice of modality depends on airway assessment and sleep-study findings.

evidence.snippet: Surveillance: At each visit: measurement of growth parameters; evaluation of nutritional status; assessment for constipation; evaluation for new neurologic features and seizure activity with EEG follow up as indicated
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews specifies the recurring multisystem surveillance domains.

evidence.snippet: Dental evaluation every six months after the eruption of primary teeth.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews gives a specific dental surveillance interval.

treatments/11.description: Surveillance should track growth, nutrition, constipation, neurologic and seizure findings, signs of medullary compression or arrhythmia, developmental progress, behavior, physical skills, and recurrent infections. GeneReviews also recommends six-monthly dental review after primary-tooth eruption and annual or clinically indicated ophthalmologic evaluation.

evidence.snippet: Loss of the MLL/WDR5 complex affects microtubule nucleation and regrowth. MLL/WDR5 localize to the pericentriolar material and interact with centriolar satellite protein Cep72 and γ-tubulin ring complex proteins (γ-TuRCs).
evidence.explanation: The study establishes the centrosomal cellular phenotype underlying this emerging mechanistic branch.

hypotheses/0.description: Proposes that loss of a non-nuclear KMT2A/MLL-WDR5 function at centrosomes contributes to neurodevelopmental manifestations through impaired recruitment of Cep72 and gamma-tubulin ring-complex proteins. The cellular phenotype is reported in WSS-derived cells, but its contribution to individual clinical manifestations has not been quantified.

evidence.snippet: Despite opposite enzymatic activities, the two mouse models deficient for either Kmt2a or Kdm5c shared reduced dendritic spines and increased aggression.
evidence.explanation: The Kmt2a-heterozygous mouse supplies the principal evidence for this neuronal branch.

hypotheses/1.description: Proposes that KMT2A-dependent, locus-specific H3K4 methylation and transcriptional changes alter dendritic spine biology and contribute to the human neurodevelopmental phenotype. Evidence currently comes primarily from constitutive Kmt2a-heterozygous mice and therefore requires confirmation in human developmental neural models.

evidence.snippet: First, we measured gene expression and H3K4me3 in adult brain tissues, a mixture of many neuron and glia types, which may mask potentially important molecular changes.
evidence.explanation: The authors explicitly identify adult mixed brain tissue as a limitation.

evidence.snippet: It is important to note that the double mutations introduced in our mice were constitutive, and therefore a lifetime of adaptation to loss of these two major chromatin regulators may occur from early developmental stages.
evidence.explanation: The study acknowledges developmental adaptation in its constitutive genetic design.

open_questions/0.rationale: The mouse study provides the main experimental bridge from KMT2A dosage to dendritic morphology, but the molecular assays used adult amygdala tissue containing mixed neuronal and glial populations, only male mice were studied, and the constitutive genotype permits lifetime adaptation. Global H3K4me1-3 levels were not dramatically altered, and Kmt2a-heterozygous mice were normal in the two learning/memory assays used. The model therefore supports a locus-specific neuronal hypothesis, not a direct equivalence to human intellectual disability or a global histone-methylation-loss mechanism.

evidence.snippet: WDSTS episignature enabled classification of variants of uncertain significance in the KMT2A gene as well as confirmation of diagnosis in patients with clinical presentation of WDSTS without known genetic variants.
evidence.explanation: The discovery cohort demonstrates positive clinical utility.

evidence.snippet: Remaining Cornelia de Lange syndrome, KMT2A, KDM5C and CHD7 signatures reached 70–100% sensitivity at best with unstable performances, suffering from heterogeneous methylation profiles among cases and rare discordant samples.
evidence.explanation: Independent testing motivates the open interpretation question.

open_questions/1.rationale: The discovery study showed clinical utility for variant classification, but independent evaluation found KMT2A sensitivity ranging from 70% to 100% at best with unstable performance and heterogeneous methylation profiles. The assay is useful as supporting functional evidence, yet its negative predictive value and handling of intermediate profiles remain insufficiently standardized for exclusionary use.

evidence.snippet: the variants in the nucleotide-binding domain (NBD) and in between the NBD and LRR are associated with Blau syndrome and NAID, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Locates the NAID/YAOS-associated variants in the NBD region, distinct from Crohn LRR variants.

evidence.snippet: Approximately one in five people is heterozygous for c.2717+158C>T in the gnomAD database, while one in 12 is heterozygous for p.Arg702Trp in gnomAD.
evidence.explanation: The population carrier frequency of the defining alleles far exceeds any plausible disease prevalence, arguing against them being disease-defining.

steps/4.description: Germline low-frequency, low-penetrance NOD2 variants - chiefly the deep-intronic IVS8+158 and the missense R702W, alone or co-inherited, with additional L1007fs and V955I - are the genetic substrate of YAOS. They are modeled as susceptibility rather than deterministic alleles because they are common in the general population and most carriers never develop disease. YAOS-associated coding variants cluster in and around the central nucleotide-binding domain, distinct from the LRR-region variants that predispose to Crohn disease.

evidence.snippet: NOD2 transcript level and basal p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) activity were significantly elevated in PBMCs from IVS8+158 YAOS patients.
evidence.explanation: Directly demonstrates elevated NOD2 expression and p38 MAPK activity in patient cells.

evidence.snippet: Intron-8 splicing of NOD2 transcripts was unaffected by carriage of NOD2 IVS8+158.
evidence.explanation: The intronic allele does not act through altered splicing, so its functional mechanism remains undefined.

evidence.snippet: Compared with HCs, P-RIP2, p-p65, p-p38, p-ERK, and p-JNK notably increased in PBMCs of a patient with YAOS.
evidence.explanation: Shows hyperphosphorylation across the NOD2-RIP2-MAPK/NF-kappaB cascade.

evidence.snippet: NOD2 Q902K-transfected cells did not demonstrate an increase in basal and MDP-stimulated NF-κB activity when compared to wild-type NOD2
evidence.explanation: A reconstitution assay found no NF-kappaB gain of function for Q902K, qualifying any simple activating-allele model.

evidence.snippet: Nod2 stimulation with muramyl dipeptide (MDP) led to a nuclear accumulation of c-Rel NF-kB subunit.
evidence.explanation: Model-organism evidence that NOD2 engages NF-kappaB, supporting the pathway node rather than the human phenotype.

steps/5.description: NOD2 senses bacterial muramyl dipeptide and signals through RIP2 to activate p38 MAPK and canonical NF-kappaB. In YAOS peripheral blood mononuclear cells NOD2 transcript level and basal p38 MAPK activity are elevated, and phospho-RIP2, p65 and p38 are increased in patient cells and tissues. Signaling is genotype-divergent: MDP-stimulated NF-kappaB activity and TNF secretion are suppressed in the IVS8+158/R702W haplotype, so the disease cannot be reduced to uniform NOD2 gain of function.

evidence.snippet: these patients' cells had elevated basal IL-6 secretion that was enhanced by muramyl dipeptide (MDP) stimulation.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates elevated and MDP-inducible IL-6 secretion in patient PBMCs.

evidence.snippet: Serum interleukin (IL)-6 level along with tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α and IL-6 secreted from PBMCs were markedly higher in patients with YAOS in comparison to healthy controls (HCs).
evidence.explanation: Independent patient data showing elevated IL-6 and TNF.

evidence.snippet: The supernatants of synovial cells from a patient with YAOS showed substantially higher IL-1β and IL-6 levels than those of RA and OA.
evidence.explanation: Places the cytokine excess in the joint compartment above disease controls.

evidence.snippet: Resembling other SAIDs, plasma levels of TNFα, IL-1β, IL-6, IFNγ, and S100A12 were unaltered in YAOS patients.
evidence.explanation: Baseline plasma cytokines were not elevated, contradicting a persistent systemic cytokine excess.

steps/6.description: Aberrant NOD2 signaling drives excess proinflammatory cytokine production, most prominently IL-6, with contributions from IL-1beta and TNF. Basal and MDP-enhanced IL-6 secretion is elevated in IVS8+158 carriers, providing the rationale for IL-6 and IL-1 blockade. Resting plasma cytokine levels can be normal, so the dysregulation is most evident on cellular stimulation rather than as a persistent systemic elevation.

evidence.snippet: These patients characteristically presented with periodic fever, dermatitis and inflammatory polyarthritis.
evidence.explanation: The founding cohort defines the core multi-organ autoinflammatory presentation.

evidence.snippet: Yao syndrome (YAOS), a recently reported novel disease, possesses characteristic clinical pattern or constellation of recurrent fever, dermatitis, arthralgia, distal leg swelling, gastrointestinal, sicca-like symptoms, and eyelid swelling among others.
evidence.explanation: Recent review enumerating the multi-organ constellation modeled by this node.

steps/7.description: Cytokine-driven sterile innate-immune inflammation produces recurrent self-limited multi-organ flares affecting skin, joints, gastrointestinal tract, serosal surfaces and periorbital and distal-limb soft tissue, together with fever and elevated acute-phase reactants, without high-titer autoantibodies. Flares generally do not progress to irreversible organ damage.

evidence.snippet: Nectin-1 is a cell-cell adhesion molecule that is important for the initial step in the formation of adherens junctions and tight junctions; it is expressed in keratinocytes, neurons, and the developing face and palate

evidence.snippet: In patient keratinocytes, mutated nectin-4 lost its capability to bind nectin-1. evidence.explanation: Supports nectin-4/nectin-1 interaction in a related PVRL4 nectinopathy; it does not establish a NECTIN1 hair, tooth, nail, or sweat-gland chain.

steps/2.description: PVRL1 (NECTIN1) encodes nectin-1, an immunoglobulin-related transmembrane cell-cell adhesion molecule that is part of the NAP cell adhesion system. Nectin-1 is important for the initial step in adherens-junction and tight-junction formation. The four PVRL1 variants reported through 2015 produced truncated proteins lacking the transmembrane and intracellular domains required to initiate nectin-1-mediated adhesion. In the related PVRL4-associated ectodermal dysplasia-syndactyly syndrome, mutant nectin-4 loses its ability to bind nectin-1 and alters junction-complex localization in hair follicles. This is cross-nectinopathy evidence, not direct evidence from NECTIN1-deficient appendages.

evidence.snippet: Here, we use in utero lentiviral-mediated genetic approaches in mice to provide the first direct evidence that the nectin-afadin axis is essential for proper palate shelf elevation and fusion
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the tissue-level palate mechanism in mice.

steps/3.description: Mouse experiments show that the nectin-afadin axis is required for palate shelf elevation and fusion. Palatal epithelial loss of afadin induces high-penetrance cleft palate; loss of either Nectin1 or Nectin4 produces mild palate-closure defects at low penetrance, and combined loss produces severe cleft palate. Expression of human NECTIN1 W185X in mice causes cleft palate with greater penetrance than Nectin1 loss, suggesting a dominant interfering mechanism in that model.

evidence.snippet: After histopathological diagnosis and eventually a maximal safe resection, patients with good prognostic factors may be followed by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
evidence.explanation: This treatment review supports maximal safe resection as a core early management step for astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas, the modern entities replacing most legacy oligoastrocytomas.

treatments/0.description: Initial management typically includes maximal safe surgical resection for diagnosis, cytoreduction, symptom relief, and tissue acquisition for integrated molecular testing.

evidence.snippet: diffuse astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas are mainly treated with combined radiochemotherapy or maximal safe resection followed by combined radiochemotherapy according to current guidelines based on randomized trials.
evidence.explanation: The treatment review supports radiotherapy as part of combined treatment for diffuse astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas.

treatments/1.description: Radiation therapy is used based on integrated molecular diagnosis, grade, residual disease, risk profile, and timing relative to chemotherapy or observation.

evidence.snippet: In patients with anaplastic oligodendroglial tumors with 1p/19q codeletion, probable 20-year overall survival following radiotherapy without vs with the combination of procarbazine, lomustine, and vincristine was 13.6% vs 37.1%
evidence.explanation: This adult brain malignancy review summarizes randomized-trial evidence for PCV chemotherapy with radiotherapy in 1p/19q-codeleted anaplastic oligodendroglial tumors, relevant to the oligodendroglioma arm of legacy oligoastrocytoma reclassification.

treatments/2.description: Alkylating chemotherapy such as temozolomide or the PCV regimen is selected according to the reassigned molecular entity, tumor grade, and clinical risk profile.

evidence.snippet: In patients with grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma, vorasidenib significantly improved progression-free survival and delayed the time to the next intervention.
evidence.explanation: The phase 3 INDIGO trial directly supports vorasidenib as an IDH-directed therapy for selected grade 2 IDH-mutant gliomas.

treatments/3.description: Vorasidenib is an oral brain-penetrant mutant IDH1/2 inhibitor that may delay progression and subsequent anticancer intervention in selected residual or recurrent grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma after surgery only. This is not specific to historical oligoastrocytoma but is relevant to the IDH-mutant diffuse gliomas that replaced the legacy category.

evidence.snippet: Vorasidenib, an oral brain-penetrant inhibitor of mutant IDH1 and IDH2 enzymes, showed preliminary activity in IDH-mutant gliomas.
evidence.explanation: The INDIGO trial abstract supports vorasidenib as an inhibitor of mutant IDH1 and IDH2 enzymes.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Vorasidenib inhibits mutant IDH1/2 enzymatic activity.
